explanation.summary: This infant has moderate bronchiolitis with hypoxia (SpO2 89 percent) and increased work of breathing but is alert with adequate perfusion. RCH CPG mandates low-flow nasal prong oxygen (1-2 L/min) titrated to an SpO2 target of 90 percent as first-line. HFNC is escalation therapy after a documented low-flow failure. This shifts practice away from earlier North American 92-94 percent targets and pre-emptive HFNC.
key_points: Low-flow nasal prong 1-2 L/min is first-line oxygen delivery for bronchiolitis at RCH
SpO2 target is at least 90 percent, not 92-94 percent
HFNC is reserved for failure of low-flow after 2 hours
Salbutamol is not routinely recommended in bronchiolitis under 12 months
explanation.pearls: Escalating to HFNC before trialling low-flow for 2 hours over-medicalises stable bronchiolitis; document the low-flow trial before you step up.

options.rationale: Bronchodilators are not recommended in bronchiolitis in this age group and driving oxygen through a nebuliser is not the correct route. Salbutamol has not been shown to alter the natural history of bronchiolitis and RCH recommends against routine use. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

HFNC is not first-line in RCH-aligned practice; it is escalation therapy for infants who fail low-flow after 2 hours. Starting HFNC immediately in a child who has not yet had a low-flow trial is over-escalation. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

The RCH SpO2 target in bronchiolitis is 90 percent, not 94 percent, because higher targets prolong length of stay without benefit. Face mask delivery is also poorly tolerated by infants and is not the standard first-line device. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

CPAP is a paediatric intensive care escalation used for impending respiratory failure not responsive to HFNC. It is not indicated as the initial oxygen device on the general ward. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

RCH CPG for bronchiolitis specifies low-flow nasal prong oxygen (1-2 L/min) as first-line for hypoxia, with a target SpO2 of 90 percent. HFNC is reserved for failure of low-flow after 2 hours of observation. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

explanation.summary: Mild croup at RCH is treated with oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg per kg as a single dose, not the severe-croup 0.6 mg per kg dose. The severity tier is decided by rest stridor and work of breathing at rest, not stridor with agitation. All severity tiers get a steroid dose because it reduces relapse and re-presentation.
key_points: Mild and moderate croup: dexamethasone 0.15 mg per kg orally single dose
Severe croup with rest stridor: 0.6 mg per kg orally, plus nebulised adrenaline
Nebulised budesonide is reserved for children unable to tolerate oral
Prednisolone has higher relapse and is not first-line at RCH
explanation.pearls: Stridor with agitation but not at rest is mild croup - 0.15 mg per kg dexamethasone once is enough.

options.rationale: This child has mild croup (Westley 1-2) - stridor with agitation only, no rest stridor, minimal recession. RCH CPG specifies oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg per kg for mild and moderate croup; the higher 0.6 mg per kg dose is reserved for severe croup with rest stridor and marked recession. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

0.6 mg per kg is the severe croup dose. Using it for mild croup delivers four times the required steroid load without added benefit in mild disease, and this child has no rest stridor. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

Nebulised budesonide is second-line and used when oral is not tolerated (persistent vomiting, unable to swallow). Oral dexamethasone is preferred first-line at RCH because it is cheaper, longer-acting, and does not require agitation with a mask. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

Prednisolone has shorter duration than dexamethasone and higher relapse rates in croup; RCH prefers dexamethasone. Prednisolone is a legitimate alternative only when dexamethasone is unavailable. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

Mild croup still benefits from a single dose of dexamethasone (reduced re-presentation and symptom duration); RCH recommends steroid for all severity tiers of croup. Withholding delays benefit and misses discharge on the same visit. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

explanation.summary: Rest stridor with a widespread urticarial rash after peanut exposure is anaphylaxis by ASCIA criteria. First-line is IM adrenaline into the anterolateral thigh at the banded weight dose - 150 mcg for 7.5-20 kg and 300 mcg for over 20 kg. Australian practice deliberately avoids mg per kg arithmetic for adrenaline in anaphylaxis to reduce dosing errors.
key_points: Anaphylaxis: IM adrenaline to anterolateral thigh, first-line
ASCIA banded dose: 150 mcg for 7.5-20 kg (EpiPen Jr); 300 mcg for over 20 kg (EpiPen)
Do not calculate mg per kg during the resuscitation
Nebulised adrenaline is adjunct, never a substitute
explanation.pearls: Banded weight tables save lives when the calculator is slow - 15 kg gets 150 mcg without arithmetic.

options.rationale: 300 mcg is the ASCIA banded dose for children over 20 kg (EpiPen adult). At 15 kg this doubles the correct dose and increases risk of tachyarrhythmia. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines 2023)

ASCIA banded dosing for children 7.5-20 kg is adrenaline 150 mcg IM (0.15 mL of 1:1000). This child is 15 kg and sits squarely in the 7.5-20 kg band. Using the banded table rather than mg per kg arithmetic reduces dose error under time pressure. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines 2023)

The ASCIA standard is a banded weight table, not per-kg calculation, precisely to avoid arithmetic errors during a resuscitation. Although 10 mcg per kg happens to give the same answer at 15 kg, teaching or documenting per-kg arithmetic in adrenaline for anaphylaxis is discouraged in AU practice. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines 2023)
Subcutaneous absorption is slower and less predictable than intramuscular in shock; ASCIA and ANZCOR require IM into the anterolateral thigh. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines 2023)

Nebulised adrenaline may be added as adjunct for upper airway oedema after IM adrenaline is given, but never as a substitute for the first IM dose. Nebulised alone does not treat systemic anaphylaxis. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines 2023)

explanation.summary: A neonate presenting hypotonic, poorly perfused, hypoglycaemic and acidotic after a fever at home has septic shock until proven otherwise. RCH pathway for infants under 28 days combines cefotaxime (not ceftriaxone) plus benzylpenicillin for Listeria cover, IV dextrose 10 percent 2 mL per kg for hypoglycaemia, and 20 mL per kg normal saline boluses. LP is performed once stabilised so as not to delay first-dose antibiotics.
key_points: Neonates under 28 days: cefotaxime plus benzylpenicillin (not ceftriaxone)
Correct hypoglycaemia with 10 percent dextrose 2 mL per kg
Fluid boluses 20 mL per kg over 5 to 10 minutes, repeat to 60 mL per kg then inotropes
LP after stabilisation - never before first-dose antibiotics in a shocked infant
explanation.pearls: Ceftriaxone is a paediatric go-to but is contraindicated in the neonate for bilirubin and calcium reasons - swap to cefotaxime under 28 days.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Sepsis assessment and management
eTG complete: Neonatal sepsis empirical therapy

options.rationale: This infant is not agitated; he is hypotonic and shocked. Sedation would worsen respiratory drive and cardiovascular status. Oral rehydration cannot address septic shock. (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis assessment and management)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Sepsis assessment and management

options.rationale: Ceftriaxone is contraindicated in neonates because of bilirubin displacement and calcium precipitation risk; cefotaxime is the third-generation cephalosporin of choice under 28 days. This choice also omits benzylpenicillin for Listeria and does not correct the documented hypoglycaemia. (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis assessment and management)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Sepsis assessment and management

options.rationale: Amoxicillin plus gentamicin is a legitimate early neonatal regimen but at 21 days the RCH pathway shifts to cefotaxime plus benzylpenicillin because meningitis pathogen spectrum broadens. LP should not delay first-dose antibiotics or fluid resuscitation in a shocked infant; do LP after stabilisation. (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis assessment and management)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Sepsis assessment and management

options.rationale: This is a shocked hypoglycaemic neonate. RCH neonatal sepsis pathway for infants under 28 days requires IV access, blood cultures, and empirical broad-spectrum IV antibiotics within the hour (cefotaxime plus benzylpenicillin for Listeria cover), correction of hypoglycaemia with 2 mL per kg of 10 percent dextrose, and fluid resuscitation with 20 mL per kg boluses. (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis assessment and management)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Sepsis assessment and management

options.rationale: Withholding antibiotics in a shocked neonate would result in preventable death; first-dose antibiotics are targeted within the hour. Cultures inform, not gate, antibiotic timing. (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis assessment and management)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Sepsis assessment and management

explanation.summary: This girl meets classical Kawasaki criteria (fever plus 4 of 5 principal features), has supportive labs (raised CRP, thrombocytosis, hypoalbuminaemia, sterile pyuria, hyponatraemia, anaemia, transaminitis) and borderline coronary dilatation. Even beyond day 10, if inflammation or coronary changes persist, IVIG 2 g per kg plus aspirin remains indicated because coronary morbidity continues to accrue.
key_points: Late-presenting Kawasaki still warrants IVIG if ongoing inflammation or coronary changes
IVIG dose is 2 g per kg over 10 to 12 hours as a single infusion
Aspirin is added at anti-inflammatory dose in the acute phase, then reduced to antiplatelet
Steroid is adjunctive for high-risk or IVIG-refractory disease, not a substitute
explanation.pearls: Kawasaki does not have a day-10 IVIG cut-off - if CRP is still up or the coronaries are dilating, give IVIG.

options.rationale: Corticosteroid monotherapy is not first-line; adjunctive steroid is considered in IVIG-resistant disease or high-risk primary treatment, but always in combination with IVIG, not as a substitute. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

Antiplatelet aspirin alone under-treats active disease; without IVIG the coronary risk continues to accrue while systemic inflammation persists (CRP still 78, platelets 620). Follow-up echo is appropriate but is not the current management priority. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

This is late-presenting Kawasaki disease meeting classical criteria with laboratory support and borderline coronary Z-scores. Even after day 10, if there is ongoing inflammation (raised CRP or platelets) or coronary abnormality, IVIG plus aspirin is still indicated. Australian and international consensus supports IVIG in late presenters with these findings. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

The disease is not over just because desquamation has begun; coronary complications develop after the acute phase in untreated Kawasaki. NSAIDs do not modify coronary risk. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

Fever resolution without treatment is not reassurance in Kawasaki disease. Coronary aneurysms develop over subsequent weeks; discharging without IVIG in a case with ongoing inflammation is a serious under-treatment. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

explanation.summary: In a shocked child with a purpuric rash and two failed IV attempts, the next step is intraosseous access with blood cultures drawn from the trocar, followed by IV ceftriaxone and a 20 mL per kg saline bolus. ANZCOR paediatric ALS sets a 90 second window for IV before moving to IO in the critical child.
key_points: IO after 90 seconds of failed IV in a critical child
Blood cultures can be drawn from the IO trocar
Empiric IV ceftriaxone 50 mg per kg for suspected meningococcal disease over 28 days
First fluid bolus 20 mL per kg over 5 to 10 min, repeat to 60 mL per kg before inotropes
explanation.pearls: IO is the emergency access route in shocked children - 90 seconds of failed IV is enough, do not keep trying.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Sepsis assessment and management
ANZCOR Guideline 12.5 Paediatric advanced life support

options.rationale: CVL insertion is skill dependent and takes 15 to 20 minutes in a shocked small child in a rural ED; it is not the emergency access route. IO is faster and safer under these conditions. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline 12.5)
source_refs: ANZCOR Guideline 12.5 Paediatric advanced life support

options.rationale: ANZCOR sets a 90 second failure window for IV in a critical child before moving to IO, not a further 5 minutes. Prolonging IV attempts in a shocked child delays antibiotics and fluid resuscitation and increases mortality. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline 12.5)
source_refs: ANZCOR Guideline 12.5 Paediatric advanced life support

options.rationale: In a shocked child with meningococcal features and two failed IV attempts within a few minutes, IO access is the next step by ANZCOR paediatric ALS. Blood cultures may be drawn from the IO trocar; do not delay first-dose IV antibiotic and fluid resuscitation. Ceftriaxone at 50 mg per kg is empiric for suspected meningococcal disease over 28 days. (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis assessment and management)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Sepsis assessment and management

options.rationale: IM route in a shocked child has erratic absorption due to poor peripheral perfusion; the drug will not reach therapeutic levels in time. IO gives immediate central circulation delivery. (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis assessment and management)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Sepsis assessment and management

options.rationale: Antipyretic does not treat sepsis and fever reduction is not the driver of tachycardia in septic shock. Delaying antibiotics for symptomatic control worsens outcome. (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis assessment and management)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Sepsis assessment and management

explanation.summary: A known CAH child with vomiting, drowsiness, hypotension, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and hypoglycaemia has adrenal crisis. Parenteral hydrocortisone stress dose is required immediately - dexamethasone will not do the job because it lacks the mineralocorticoid activity needed to correct the hyperkalaemia and hyponatraemia. Simultaneous glucose correction and fluid resuscitation are life-saving.
key_points: Adrenal crisis stress dose IV hydrocortisone: 25 mg under 1 y, 50 mg 1-5 y, 100 mg over 5 y
Hydrocortisone has mineralocorticoid activity at stress doses; dexamethasone does not
Correct hypoglycaemia with 10 percent dextrose 2 mL per kg, resuscitate with normal saline 20 mL per kg
Hyperkalaemia in adrenal crisis usually corrects with hydrocortisone and fluid, not insulin dextrose
explanation.pearls: Dexamethasone is the classic wrong answer in adrenal crisis - it does not touch the mineralocorticoid deficit driving the electrolyte derangement.

options.rationale: The child is already vomiting the oral hydrocortisone; that route has failed. Oral cannot be relied on in a crisis - parenteral hydrocortisone is required, and observation alone is inadequate treatment. (Source: RCH CPG: Adrenal crisis)

Dexamethasone lacks mineralocorticoid activity and cannot correct hyperkalaemia and hyponatraemia in an adrenal crisis; hydrocortisone is required for its mineralocorticoid effect at stress doses. Oral rehydration cannot correct dehydration and hypoglycaemia here. (Source: RCH CPG: Adrenal crisis)

Insulin dextrose is inappropriate first-line in adrenal crisis with hypoglycaemia and may cause severe rebound; the hyperkalaemia here is driven by mineralocorticoid deficiency and reverses with hydrocortisone and fluid. Calcium is only indicated for ECG changes attributable to hyperkalaemia. (Source: RCH CPG: Hyperkalaemia)

Hypertonic saline is reserved for severe symptomatic hyponatraemia (seizure or coma) with truly hypotonic hyponatraemia. Adrenal crisis hyponatraemia corrects with hydrocortisone and normal saline; hypertonic saline risks osmotic demyelination and is not indicated here. (Source: RCH CPG: Hyponatraemia)

This is adrenal crisis with documented hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia. Immediate parenteral hydrocortisone stress dose (50 mg for 1-5 years, 100 mg for over 5 years, 25 mg for under 1 year) is life-saving; oral cannot be relied on because he is vomiting. Glucose correction with 10 percent dextrose 2 mL per kg and volume resuscitation with normal saline are simultaneous priorities. (Source: RCH CPG: Adrenal crisis)

explanation.summary:
Oxygen in acute asthma is a drug with a target range. Australian guidance sets saturations of 92 to 95 percent in children and titrates the delivery device down as the child improves, because routinely driving saturations to 100 percent has no benefit and can blunt the hypoxic drive and mask deterioration. Oxygen-driven nebulisers deliver a high inspired fraction as a side effect, so saturations often sit well above target during a bronchodilator burst and should be reviewed between doses.

In context: saturation targets are condition specific in paediatrics. Bronchiolitis in infants is managed to a threshold of 90 percent, acute asthma to 92 to 95 percent, and resuscitation of a shocked or peri-arrest child uses high flow oxygen until stability returns. Carrying one number across all three is a common source of both over-treatment and under-treatment.
key_points: Target saturations of 92 to 95 percent in children with acute asthma
Oxygen-driven nebulisers deliver high inspired oxygen incidentally
Wean the delivery device as work of breathing settles
Bronchiolitis and asthma have different saturation thresholds
explanation.pearls: A saturation of 100 percent on oxygen is information you have thrown away; titrate into the target range so a fall is visible early.

options.rationale: The Australian Asthma Handbook advises titrating supplemental oxygen to saturations of 92 to 95 percent in children, since higher targets confer no benefit and may worsen carbon dioxide retention. (Source: Australian Asthma Handbook)

High flow face mask oxygen is appropriate in the first minutes of resuscitation of a critically hypoxaemic or peri-arrest child, then weaned to a target range once saturations recover. (Source: Australian Asthma Handbook)

A permissive target in the high eighties belongs to acute bronchiolitis and to adults with chronic carbon dioxide retention, not to a school-aged child with asthma. (Source: Australian Asthma Handbook; RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

High flow nasal cannula is an escalation for a child with worsening work of breathing despite maximal therapy, usually in a high dependency setting. This girl is improving. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma acute)

Stopping oxygen without titration is reasonable only once the child is comfortably above target in room air, and an hourly review is too infrequent during back-to-back bronchodilators. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma acute)

explanation.summary: A febrile infant under 1 month is treated as high-risk for serious bacterial infection irrespective of appearance. RCH mandates a full septic workup (blood, urine by catheter or SPA, and CSF) alongside empirical IV benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin without delay. Ceftriaxone monotherapy is inappropriate under 1 month due to bilirubin displacement and insufficient listeria cover. Deferring LP is reserved for true instability, coagulopathy, or raised intracranial pressure.
key_points: Under 28 days: full septic workup plus empirical antibiotics for any fever
First-line empirical regimen is benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin (or cefotaxime plus benzylpenicillin)
Ceftriaxone monotherapy is avoided under 1 month
Viral positive result does NOT rule out concurrent bacterial infection in this age
explanation.pearls: In a neonate with fever, blood cultures and empirical benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin should be delivered within the hour; procedure delays never justify pushing antibiotics past 60 minutes.

sources.label: eTG complete: Neonatal sepsis empirical therapy

options.rationale: A febrile infant under 28 days is high-risk regardless of appearance and requires a full septic workup plus empirical antibiotics without waiting to see the trajectory. Observation windows apply to well-appearing infants over 60 days in some risk-tool pathways, not to neonates. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child)

RCH mandates a full septic workup with LP and empirical IV benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin (or cefotaxime) for any febrile infant under 1 month, particularly one who is unwell-appearing. Antibiotics must not be delayed beyond an hour by procedure attempts. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child)

The infant is haemodynamically stable enough to undergo LP alongside blood and urine sampling; deferring the LP means empirical treatment could not later be shortened based on CSF and risks missing meningitis. LP is only deferred in true haemodynamic instability, coagulopathy, or raised intracranial pressure. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child)

Ceftriaxone as monotherapy under 1 month is avoided in Australian paediatric practice because of bilirubin displacement and inadequate listeria cover; the RCH neonatal sepsis regimen is benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin (or cefotaxime plus benzylpenicillin). (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child)

In a febrile infant under 28 days a positive viral swab does not exclude serious bacterial infection and cannot defer antibiotics; the RCH pathway is empirical treatment for all, with de-escalation guided by cultures and CSF, not by viral testing. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child)

explanation.summary: This child has mild to moderate dehydration that failed the trial of oral rehydration. RCH pathway escalates to nasogastric ORS at approximately 25 mL/kg/hour for 4 hours before considering IV fluids. NGT rehydration is non-inferior to IV, less invasive, and preserves gut function. IV is reserved for severe dehydration, shock, or NGT failure. Ondansetron may be a useful adjunct but the weight-banded dose is 2 mg for 8-15 kg, not 4 mg.
key_points: NGT ORS is first-line when oral fails and the child is mild-moderate dehydrated
IV fluids reserved for severe dehydration, shock, or NGT failure
Ondansetron weight bands: 8-15 kg gets 2 mg, 15-30 kg gets 4 mg
Isotonic (0.9%) not third-normal saline is standard IV maintenance in AU paediatric practice
explanation.pearls: For a vomiting toddler with mild-moderate dehydration, an NGT delivering 25 mL/kg/hour of ORS beats jumping to a cannula; save the drip for shock or NGT failure.

options.rationale: This child has mild to moderate dehydration without shock (warm peripheries, capillary refill 2 seconds, alert). RCH reserves rapid IV fluid bolus for severe dehydration or shock; earlier escalation adds cannulation morbidity without benefit. (Source: RCH CPG: Dehydration)

IV maintenance-plus-deficit is used when the child is severely dehydrated or NGT rehydration has failed; RCH avoids IV as first-line for mild to moderate dehydration and one third normal saline is not the recommended paediatric maintenance fluid because of hyponatraemia risk. (Source: RCH CPG: Dehydration)

Ondansetron helps break vomiting but the RCH ondansetron dose for a 12 kg child is 2 mg, not 4 mg (2 mg for 8-15 kg, 4 mg for 15-30 kg). The pathway is right but the dose is wrong for his weight. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

Watchful observation without active rehydration prolongs deficit correction and risks progression; RCH escalates directly from failed oral to NGT within the ED assessment window rather than waiting hours to review. (Source: RCH CPG: Dehydration)

RCH first-line rehydration for mild to moderate dehydration that fails oral is nasogastric ORS, typically 25 mL/kg/hour for 4 hours or over the deficit period. NGT rehydration is non-inferior to IV, less resource-intense, and preserves gut function. (Source: RCH CPG: Dehydration)

explanation.summary: This is moderate croup (stridor at rest, mild recession, no exhaustion or hypoxia). RCH pathway is oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg as a single dose with 3 hours of observation before discharge. The 0.6 mg/kg dose is reserved for severe croup with impending respiratory failure. Nebulised adrenaline is added only for severe croup or if moderate croup deteriorates despite steroid. Nebulised budesonide is a second-line steroid route.
key_points: 0.15 mg/kg oral dexamethasone for mild to moderate croup
0.6 mg/kg oral dexamethasone reserved for severe croup
Observe 3 hours after last treatment before discharge
Nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000 flat dose is escalation, not first-line
explanation.pearls: Use 0.6 mg/kg dexamethasone only when respiratory failure is impending; the 0.15 mg/kg dose is the RCH default for stridor at rest without exhaustion.

options.rationale: RCH recommends oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg single dose for mild to moderate croup and reserves 0.6 mg/kg for severe croup with impending respiratory failure. Stridor at rest with mild recession fits the moderate band. Observation for 3 hours after last treatment is standard before discharge. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

The 0.6 mg/kg dose is reserved for severe croup with marked recession, agitation, or hypoxia; using it here overdoses a moderate case without additional benefit and unnecessary admission adds cost. Discharge home after 3 hours of stability is appropriate for moderate croup. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

Nebulised budesonide is second-line when oral dexamethasone is not tolerated; oral dexamethasone is preferred because it is systemic, well-absorbed, and cheaper. Sixty minutes is also too short an observation period for moderate croup with stridor at rest. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

Prednisolone 1 mg/kg has been used in some settings but has a shorter duration of action than dexamethasone and higher rates of representation. RCH lists dexamethasone as first-line and prednisolone as a fall-back if dexamethasone is unavailable. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

Nebulised adrenaline in RCH pathway is reserved for severe croup or moderate croup deteriorating despite steroid, not for a first presentation of stable moderate croup at initial triage. Steroid alone is enough for stridor at rest without hypoxia or exhaustion. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

explanation.summary: This child had a typical first UTI (E coli, rapid response, no red flags) with normal antenatal renal tract monitoring. RCH cascade does NOT recommend routine imaging in this scenario; ultrasound is reserved for atypical UTI (poor response after 48 hours, non-E coli, sepsis, abdominal mass, or raised creatinine) or recurrent UTI. DMSA and MCUG are NICE constructs, not part of the RCH cascade. NICE-derived teaching contradicts the local Australian pathway on this point.
key_points: RCH: no routine imaging after single typical UTI with normal antenatal scans
US indicated for atypical UTI or recurrent UTI (not routine)
DMSA and MCUG are NICE constructs, not in the RCH cascade
Atypical criteria: poor response 48 hours, non-E coli, sepsis, mass, raised creatinine
explanation.pearls: When a first UTI is E coli, rapid to respond, and follows normal antenatal scans, RCH stops at reassurance; NICE would over-image. Cite RCH to justify no imaging.

options.rationale: DMSA is not part of the RCH cascade for a single typical UTI; it is a NICE construct with limited evidence for changing management. RCH follows a stepped ultrasound-then-consider-MCUG pathway only in atypical or recurrent presentations, not routinely. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

This is the NICE construct of universal imaging in children under 24 months; the RCH cascade specifically states no routine ultrasound after a single typical UTI when antenatal monitoring was normal and response was rapid, even in children under 24 months. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

RCH pathway does NOT recommend routine renal ultrasound after a single typical UTI in a child over 6 months with documented antenatal renal tract monitoring and rapid clinical response. Ultrasound is reserved for atypical UTI (poor response after 48 hours, non-E coli organism, sepsis, abdominal mass, or raised creatinine) or recurrent UTI. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

MCUG is only considered in the RCH cascade after ultrasound shows an abnormality, in recurrent UTI, or in atypical presentations. It carries irradiation and catheterisation morbidity and is not routine after a typical first UTI with normal antenatal scans. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

MRI is not part of any Australian paediatric UTI pathway. It carries anaesthetic morbidity in a toddler with no benefit above ultrasound and is reserved for tertiary specialist-driven questions in structural or oncological cases. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

explanation.summary: This infant has failed a 2 hour trial of low-flow nasal prong oxygen with persistent hypoxia, marked work of breathing, recurrent apnoea, and rising pCO2. RCH permits escalation to HFNC at 2 L/kg/min in this weight bracket, still titrating to SpO2 90 percent. Apnoea plus hypercapnia mandates PICU liaison in parallel to escalation. Salbutamol has no role in bronchiolitis under 12 months. CPAP is a further escalation beyond HFNC and hypertonic saline is not part of the RCH pathway.
key_points: Low-flow trial for 2 hours is prerequisite before HFNC escalation
HFNC dose in this weight is 2 L/kg/min titrated to SpO2 90 percent
Recurrent apnoea plus rising pCO2 triggers PICU liaison
Salbutamol and hypertonic saline are not in the RCH bronchiolitis pathway
explanation.pearls: Recurrent apnoea in RSV bronchiolitis under 3 months plus hypercapnia is your PICU-call trigger; escalate to HFNC while making the call, do not wait for the transfer team to arrive.

options.rationale: Persistence of increased work of breathing plus recurrent apnoea after a full low-flow trial meets RCH criteria for escalation; continuing low-flow risks further deterioration. Low-flow above 2 L/min is also not standard because gas mixing is unreliable. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

Hypertonic saline is not part of the RCH bronchiolitis pathway and its evidence base is weak. It does not address hypoxia, recurrent apnoea, or CO2 retention. (Source: PREDICT bronchiolitis guideline 2022)

Salbutamol has consistently failed to alter the natural history of bronchiolitis in infants and is not recommended by RCH in this age group. Escalating to a bronchodilator in a hypercapnic, apnoeic infant delays effective respiratory support. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

Bubble CPAP via mask in a young infant with recurrent apnoea is escalation beyond ward capability and requires PICU input in parallel, not deferred. RCH pathway favours HFNC as the intermediate step before CPAP or intubation. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

RCH permits HFNC after documented failure of low-flow (2 hours) with persistent hypoxia, marked work of breathing, or recurrent apnoea. Dose is 2 L/kg/min in this weight bracket, titrated to the same 90 percent SpO2 target. Apnoea plus rising pCO2 mandates PICU liaison. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

explanation.summary: Anaphylaxis is a severe allergic reaction with respiratory or cardiovascular involvement, and IM adrenaline is the first and most important treatment. ASCIA doses it at 0.01 mg/kg of the 1 mg/mL (1:1000) solution to a maximum of 0.5 mg, given into the outer mid-thigh and repeated if there is no response. Autoinjectors come in fixed doses (150 microgram for 7.5 to 20 kg, 300 microgram above 20 kg), whereas in hospital the ampoule dose is drawn up by weight. The patient lies flat or with legs raised, and IV access is for fluid boluses of 20 mL/kg sodium chloride 0.9% and, if needed, an adrenaline infusion. Refractory anaphylaxis is persisting respiratory or cardiovascular compromise despite 2 appropriate IM doses.
key_points: IM adrenaline 0.01 mg/kg of 1 mg/mL (1:1000) to a maximum of 0.5 mg is 0.01 mL/kg.
The IM injection goes into the outer mid-thigh.
IV bolus adrenaline is not recommended except peri-arrest; refractory anaphylaxis gets an infusion.
Nebulised adrenaline for upper airway obstruction is an adjunct to IM adrenaline, not a substitute.
explanation.pearls: ASCIA advises laying the patient flat or with the legs slightly raised to improve venous return, and placing a pregnant woman in the left lateral position.

sources.label: ASCIA Guidelines: Acute management of anaphylaxis

options.rationale: This is a tenfold overdose: ASCIA sets IM adrenaline at 0.01 mg/kg of the 1 mg/mL solution to a maximum of 0.5 mg, which is 0.01 mL/kg. Confusing mg/kg with mL/kg, or 1:1000 with 1:10 000, is the classic adrenaline drawing-up error, and a second person checking the volume prevents it. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines: Acute management of anaphylaxis)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines: Acute management of anaphylaxis

options.rationale: The dose is right but the route is not: ASCIA and RCH give adrenaline by IM injection into the outer mid-thigh, and neither endorses the subcutaneous route. A deltoid IM injection is used only when the thigh cannot be reached. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines: Acute management of anaphylaxis; RCH CPG: Anaphylaxis)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines: Acute management of anaphylaxis

options.rationale: Stridor, wheeze, hypotension and cool peripheries after a nut exposure are severe anaphylaxis, and the first drug is IM adrenaline 0.01 mg/kg of 1 mg/mL (1:1000) to a maximum of 0.5 mg. At 18 kg that is 0.18 mg (0.18 mL), repeated if there is no response; in the community a 150 microgram autoinjector covers the 7.5 to 20 kg band. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines: Acute management of anaphylaxis; RCH CPG: Anaphylaxis)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines: Acute management of anaphylaxis

options.rationale: RCH states that IV bolus adrenaline is not recommended except in the peri-arrest setting; 0.01 mg/kg IV is the cardiac arrest dose. Anaphylaxis that persists after 2 appropriate IM doses is treated with an adrenaline infusion (1 mL of 1:1000 in 1000 mL sodium chloride 0.9%, starting at 5 mL/kg/hour). (Source: RCH CPG: Anaphylaxis)

ASCIA lists nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000 as something to consider for upper airway obstruction, but only alongside IM adrenaline. Nebulised adrenaline alone suits croup, where there is no systemic reaction and no hypotension. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines: Acute management of anaphylaxis)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines: Acute management of anaphylaxis

explanation.summary: This child has persistent septic shock after the first 20 mL/kg crystalloid bolus. The RCH pathway allows up to 60 mL/kg of crystalloid in 20 mL/kg boluses within the first hour before triggering inotropes, provided there are no signs of fluid-intolerant shock (rales, hepatomegaly, rising oxygen). Inotropes are for fluid-refractory or fluid-intolerant shock. Albumin, hydrocortisone, and early intubation are all later steps.
key_points: Up to 60 mL/kg crystalloid in the first hour for paediatric septic shock
Inotropes trigger on fluid-refractory or fluid-intolerant shock
Isotonic crystalloid first-line; albumin second-line
Hydrocortisone is for inotrope-refractory shock
explanation.pearls: In septic shock at 20 mL/kg with residual mottling and lactate still above 4, the next move is another 20 mL/kg bolus; save adrenaline for after the full 60 mL/kg unless fluid intolerance emerges.

options.rationale: RCH paediatric sepsis pathway is up to 60 mL/kg in 20 mL/kg boluses in the first hour if perfusion remains inadequate, with inotropes triggered by ongoing shock after fluid or by signs of fluid overload. This child has residual shock with cool peripheries and a falling but still elevated lactate; a second bolus is warranted before inotropes. (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis)

Inotropes are triggered by fluid-refractory shock or by fluid-intolerant shock (rales, hepatomegaly, rising oxygen requirement) not by residual shock at 20 mL/kg. Skipping the second bolus is over-escalation and misses the RCH order (fluids first, up to 60 mL/kg, then inotropes). (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis)

RCH first-line fluid is isotonic crystalloid (normal saline or Hartmann's); albumin is not first-line and is reserved for specific indications after several crystalloid boluses. Choosing albumin now deviates from the AU pathway without evidence of benefit. (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis)

Stress-dose hydrocortisone in paediatric septic shock is considered after inotrope-refractory shock, not as an early step. Giving it before completing fluid resuscitation delays effective early treatment. (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis)

This child is drowsy but rousable, maintaining airway, and oxygenating on Hudson mask; intubating during unresolved shock without preparatory fluid is risky (cardiovascular collapse on induction). Fluid resuscitate first, intubate if shock persists after full fluid and inotrope escalation. (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis)

explanation.summary: This is moderate paediatric DKA with poor perfusion but not overt shock. APEG and RCH advise a conservative 10 mL/kg saline bolus over 30-60 minutes (only 20 mL/kg if truly shocked with unrecordable pulses), then rehydration over 48 hours at an assumed 7 percent deficit minus the bolus, plus maintenance. Insulin infusion is started 1 hour after fluid at 0.05-0.1 units/kg/hr. Cerebral oedema is the feared complication and drives the conservative fluid approach. Bicarbonate is contraindicated except in life-threatening acidosis.
key_points: Initial bolus 10 mL/kg in paediatric DKA (20 mL/kg only in true shock)
Rehydrate over 48 hours (not 24) to minimise cerebral oedema risk
Insulin at 0.05-0.1 units/kg/hr, started 1 hour after fluid
Bicarbonate contraindicated except in pH <6.9 with cardiac depression
explanation.pearls: Do NOT rehydrate paediatric DKA over 24 hours; the APEG 48-hour deficit plus 10 mL/kg bolus schedule exists specifically to reduce cerebral oedema mortality.

options.rationale: The 20 mL/kg bolus is only used in true shock (systolic BP <5th centile for age, unrecordable pulses); this child has poor perfusion but a MAP within acceptable range for age. The APEG and RCH pathway uses 10 mL/kg over 30-60 minutes for the initial bolus in DKA to reduce cerebral oedema risk. (Source: APEG/RCH: Paediatric DKA)

Subcutaneous insulin is not adequate for correcting DKA in this age; IV insulin infusion is standard. Delaying any bolus is inappropriate given poor perfusion, and gastric decompression alone does not address the acidosis. (Source: APEG/RCH: Paediatric DKA)

Bicarbonate is contraindicated in paediatric DKA except in life-threatening acidosis (pH <6.9) with cardiac depression, because it worsens paradoxical CSF acidosis and cerebral oedema. Immediate insulin without fluid loading also increases cerebral oedema risk. (Source: APEG/RCH: Paediatric DKA)

Deficit replacement over 24 hours is faster than the APEG/RCH-recommended 48 hours and increases cerebral oedema risk; the initial bolus is also 10 mL/kg not 20 mL/kg unless truly shocked. Immediate insulin is again unsafe. (Source: APEG/RCH: Paediatric DKA)

APEG and RCH DKA pathway uses a conservative 10 mL/kg bolus over 30-60 min to lower cerebral oedema risk, with rehydration over 48 hours at an assumed 7 percent deficit (moderate DKA) minus the bolus, plus maintenance. Insulin is delayed by 1 hour after starting fluid and started at 0.05-0.1 units/kg/hr. (Source: APEG/RCH: Paediatric DKA)

explanation.summary: This child on day 8 of fever meets the incomplete Kawasaki disease algorithm: fever more than 5 days, 2 principal criteria (conjunctival injection, lip changes), supportive laboratory features (platelets 620, ALT 92, albumin 28, CRP 145, sterile pyuria), and a coronary Z score of 2.6. Immediate IVIG 2 g/kg plus aspirin is indicated within 10 days of fever onset to reduce coronary aneurysm risk from about 25 percent to under 5 percent. Steroid monotherapy, ongoing antibiotics, or aspirin monotherapy are all inappropriate.
key_points: Incomplete Kawasaki: fever more than 5 days plus supportive labs plus coronary Z more than 2
IVIG 2 g/kg plus aspirin is first-line and should be given within 10 days of fever onset
Coronary Z score more than 2 alone justifies treatment
Delaying past day 10 increases aneurysm risk substantially
explanation.pearls: Do not wait for the 4th and 5th principal Kawasaki criteria in an infant; incomplete Kawasaki with any coronary Z more than 2 or supportive lab profile gets IVIG within the 10-day window.

options.rationale: This is incomplete (atypical) Kawasaki disease: fever more than 5 days plus 2 principal criteria (conjunctival injection, lip changes) with supportive laboratory features (raised platelets, ALT, low albumin, sterile pyuria, raised CRP/ESR) and a coronary artery Z score more than 2. IVIG 2 g/kg is indicated within 10 days of fever onset to lower coronary aneurysm risk from about 25 percent to under 5 percent, together with aspirin. Coronary Z score 2.6 also independently supports treatment. (Source: AHA/RANZCPCH Kawasaki disease guidelines)

The incomplete Kawasaki algorithm mandates immediate treatment when fever more than 5 days plus supportive labs plus coronary changes are present, even without 4 of 5 principal criteria. Delaying past day 10 substantially raises aneurysm risk. (Source: AHA/RANZCPCH Kawasaki disease guidelines)

First-line treatment is IVIG plus aspirin. Steroids are added upfront only in Kobayashi-high-risk patients (Japanese scoring) or as adjuncts, not as monotherapy. Withholding IVIG delays effective aneurysm prevention. (Source: AHA/RANZCPCH Kawasaki disease guidelines)

There is no infectious source and the clinical picture, laboratory profile, and coronary changes point to Kawasaki disease; empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics would delay IVIG and are not appropriate. (Source: AHA/RANZCPCH Kawasaki disease guidelines)

Aspirin alone does not reduce aneurysm risk; IVIG is the aneurysm-preventing agent. Deferring for 6 weeks is well past the IVIG treatment window and would result in preventable coronary damage. (Source: AHA/RANZCPCH Kawasaki disease guidelines)

explanation.summary: Late-onset (over 48 hours) neonatal sepsis with meningitis and seizure activity in a 12-day-old requires empirical cover for GBS, E coli, other Gram negatives, listeria (still possible in the first month), and HSV. The standard AU empirical regimen is meningitic-dose IV cefotaxime (avoiding ceftriaxone under 1 month), plus IV benzylpenicillin (listeria), plus IV aciclovir 20 mg/kg 8 hourly (HSV encephalitis). Benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin alone is the early-onset neonatal sepsis regimen and does not have adequate CNS penetration.
key_points: Late-onset neonatal meningitis: IV cefotaxime meningitic dose plus benzylpenicillin plus aciclovir
Ceftriaxone avoided under 1 month due to bilirubin displacement
Aciclovir empirical cover for HSV when neonatal seizures present
Early-onset regimen (benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin) is inadequate for late-onset meningitis
explanation.pearls: In a 12-day-old with seizures and CSF pleocytosis, add IV aciclovir 20 mg/kg 8-hourly to cefotaxime and benzylpenicillin without waiting for HSV PCR; the treatment window for HSV encephalitis is measured in hours.

options.rationale: For late-onset neonatal sepsis (over 48 hours) with meningitis and confirmed CSF pleocytosis, cover must extend to meningitic doses of a cephalosporin because CNS penetration of gentamicin is limited. Benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin is the empirical early-onset (under 48 hours) neonatal sepsis regimen, not late-onset with meningitis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Neonatal sepsis)

Late-onset neonatal sepsis with meningitis in a 12-day-old requires meningitic-dose cefotaxime (for GBS, E coli, other Gram negatives) plus benzylpenicillin (adds listeria cover) plus IV aciclovir 20 mg/kg 8 hourly for empirical HSV encephalitis cover given seizure activity. Ceftriaxone is avoided under 1 month for bilirubin displacement reasons; cefotaxime is preferred. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Neonatal sepsis)

Ceftriaxone is avoided under 1 month due to bilirubin displacement and hypocalcaemia risk; cefotaxime is preferred. Vancomycin is added if there is suspicion of coagulase-negative staphylococcus (indwelling lines) which is not obvious here. HSV cover is also missing. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Neonatal sepsis)

Flucloxacillin plus gentamicin does not cover GBS, listeria, or Gram-negative meningitis adequately in this age. Dexamethasone before antibiotics is a paediatric bacterial meningitis (over 2 months) intervention and its role in neonatal meningitis is unproven. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Neonatal sepsis)

Meropenem monotherapy is not first-line empirical treatment for community-onset late-onset neonatal sepsis with meningitis; it is reserved for resistant Gram-negative sepsis or ESBL exposure. HSV cover is still needed given the seizure activity. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Neonatal sepsis)

explanation.summary: Infant bronchiolitis failing standard flow oxygen is escalated to heated humidified HFNC at 2 L/kg/min with FiO2 titrated to a target SpO2 of 92 to 96 percent. Salbutamol, adrenaline and steroids are not routine bronchiolitis therapies. Fluid boluses are reserved for shock, and intubation is a last resort after non-invasive support fails.
key_points: HFNC 2 L/kg/min is the first AU escalation for bronchiolitis with hypoxia
Bronchodilators, adrenaline and steroids do not treat classic bronchiolitis
Fluid boluses only if shocked; NG feeds preferred otherwise
Escalate to CPAP or intubate only after HFNC failure
explanation.pearls: In an infant on HFNC, heart rate that has not fallen and respiratory rate still above 60 after 60 minutes predicts HFNC failure and prompts CPAP or intubation planning.

options.rationale: AU bronchiolitis pathways use HFNC at 2 L/kg/min for infants failing standard flow oxygen with recessions and desaturation, before CPAP or intubation. FiO2 is titrated to a target SpO2 of 92 to 96 percent.
Salbutamol has no proven benefit in typical infant bronchiolitis and does not correct the ventilation deficit driving hypoxia and worsening work of breathing here.
Non-rebreather masks are poorly tolerated in infants and give no positive pressure; adrenaline and steroid are croup pathway treatments, not bronchiolitis.
There is no shock: capillary refill is 2 seconds and lactate is normal. A fluid bolus risks worsening pulmonary oedema in bronchiolitis without indication.
Intubation is premature before a trial of non-invasive escalation; PaCO2 48 with pH 7.34 is not immediate respiratory failure and HFNC or CPAP have not been tried.

explanation.summary: Australian guidance treats Aboriginal children, children under 2 years, and children with bilateral or severe acute otitis media with immediate high-dose amoxicillin for 7 days because of high risk of chronic suppurative otitis media and pneumococcal complications. Watchful waiting is only for well older children in low-risk populations. Amoxicillin-clavulanate is reserved for treatment failure at 48 to 72 hours.
key_points: Immediate amoxicillin for Aboriginal, under-2, or severe or bilateral disease
High-dose amoxicillin 30 mg/kg BD covers non-susceptible pneumococcus
Course length is 7 days in high-risk groups
Amoxicillin-clavulanate reserved for treatment failure
explanation.pearls: Always examine both TMs and note any perforation size and discharge; a perforation with discharge changes management to topical ciprofloxacin drops alongside oral amoxicillin.

sources.label: CARPA Standard Treatment Manual: Ear infections

options.rationale: Watchful waiting is inappropriate here because he is Aboriginal and remote, a group at very high risk of chronic suppurative otitis media, where immediate antibiotics are recommended.

AU guidance recommends immediate high-dose amoxicillin for 7 days in Aboriginal children, children under 2 years, or those with bilateral or severe disease. High-dose amoxicillin covers penicillin-non-susceptible pneumococcus.
For Aboriginal, remote, or under-2 children immediate high-dose amoxicillin is first line, and the standard course length in this group is 7 days rather than 5.
Amoxicillin-clavulanate is reserved for treatment failure at 48 to 72 hours or documented recurrence; high-dose amoxicillin monotherapy is first line for uncomplicated disease.
IM ceftriaxone is reserved for children unable to tolerate oral therapy or those with treatment failure; it is not first line in a well child able to take oral medication.

explanation.summary: Functional constipation with faecal loading is treated with escalating oral macrogol as first line disimpaction, titrated over 3 to 7 days until liquid stool is passed. Rectal enemas are second line and manual disimpaction under GA is rare. Investigations for organic causes are pursued only when red flags such as delayed meconium, failure to thrive, or abnormal perianal exam are present.
key_points: Escalating oral macrogol is first line disimpaction
Rectal enemas are second line, not first line
Maintenance osmotic laxatives will not clear an established impaction
Hirschsprung suspected only with delayed meconium and failure to thrive
explanation.pearls: Continue maintenance macrogol for at least 3 months after regular painless stools resume; earlier withdrawal is the commonest reason for relapse of soiling.

options.rationale: Manual disimpaction under GA is reserved for children who fail oral or rectal disimpaction after several days; oral therapy is first line and effective in most children.
Rectal enemas are second line after oral macrogol has failed or been refused; they are more distressing for the child and family and are not more effective than oral macrogol.

AU paediatric guidance recommends escalating oral macrogol as first-line disimpaction, titrated by weight and age to a ceiling around 12 sachets per day, over 3 to 7 days until liquid stool is passed.
Lactulose alone is inadequate for disimpaction; a maintenance dose osmotic laxative will not clear established faecal loading, and 4 weeks allows further soiling.
Hirschsprung disease presents with delayed meconium and failure to thrive from infancy, absent here. Imaging and biopsy are not needed to start therapy for typical functional constipation.

explanation.summary: Anaphylaxis is treated with IM adrenaline 10 microgram/kg (maximum 500 microgram) into the mid-anterolateral thigh, repeated every 5 minutes as needed. For a 22 kg child this is 220 microgram given as 0.22 mL of 1:1000. IV bolus adrenaline is arrhythmogenic and reserved for refractory cases where an infusion is being initiated in a monitored setting.
key_points: IM adrenaline 10 microgram/kg to max 500 microgram is first line
Mid-anterolateral thigh gives faster absorption than deltoid
IV bolus adrenaline carries arrhythmia risk and is not first line
Repeat IM dose at 5 minutes if inadequate response
explanation.pearls: After two IM doses without adequate response, commence a peripheral adrenaline infusion at 0.1 to 1 microgram/kg/min while awaiting central access and senior support.

sources.label: ASCIA Guidelines: Acute management of anaphylaxis

options.rationale: 150 microgram is the paediatric autoinjector for children 7.5 to 20 kg; this child is 22 kg so weight-based IM dose is 220 microgram, given as an autoinjector or 0.22 mL 1:1000.
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines: Acute management of anaphylaxis

options.rationale: IV bolus adrenaline is not first line and carries significant risk of arrhythmia and hypertensive crisis; IM adrenaline is first line and IV infusion is reserved for refractory anaphylaxis.
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines: Acute management of anaphylaxis

options.rationale: 500 microgram is the adult IM dose; the deltoid is not the preferred site because absorption is slower than the mid-anterolateral thigh.
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines: Acute management of anaphylaxis

options.rationale: Weight-based IM adrenaline for anaphylaxis is 10 microgram/kg to a maximum 500 microgram; for 22 kg this is 220 microgram (0.22 mL of 1:1000) IM into the mid-anterolateral thigh.
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines: Acute management of anaphylaxis

options.rationale: Nebulised adrenaline is not first line for anaphylaxis and does not treat cardiovascular or systemic manifestations; IM adrenaline is the standard first line therapy.
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines: Acute management of anaphylaxis

explanation.summary: In children ITP is a clinical diagnosis and platelet count alone does not drive therapy; the Buchanan bleeding score guides decisions. A well child with only cutaneous petechiae and no wet purpura or active bleeding is managed with observation, safety advice and outpatient review regardless of platelet count. Steroids, IVIG and anti-D are reserved for higher-grade bleeding phenotypes and bone marrow only if atypical.
key_points: Manage by bleeding phenotype, not by platelet count alone
Observation is first line for cutaneous-only bleeding
IVIG and steroids reserved for wet purpura or active bleeding
Bone marrow only if atypical features present
explanation.pearls: The Buchanan bleeding score grades from 0 (none) to 5 (life-threatening); scores of 3 or more (mucosal bleeding or worse) prompt IVIG or steroid therapy, not the platelet count.

options.rationale: Corticosteroids are considered for wet purpura, active bleeding, or a rising bleeding score; asymptomatic petechial disease in a well child does not warrant steroid exposure and admission.
IVIG is reserved for significant bleeding or a high bleeding risk score (wet purpura, mucosal bleeding, or planned procedure); it is not indicated in asymptomatic petechial disease.
Anti-D is limited to Rh-positive non-splenectomised children with intact haemoglobin and carries a risk of severe haemolysis; it is not first line for asymptomatic ITP in Australia.
Bone marrow examination is not required in classic ITP with a normal film, normal WCC and no atypical features; it is reserved for atypical presentations or before some centres start steroids.
AU guidance supports observation for asymptomatic or minor bleeding phenotype ITP regardless of platelet count, with head injury and wet purpura advice, in preference to routine drug therapy.

explanation.summary: DKA resolves when pH exceeds 7.3, bicarbonate 15 mmol/L, and beta-hydroxybutyrate is under 1 mmol/L, with the child alert and tolerating oral intake. Transition is achieved by giving subcutaneous basal insulin (glargine or detemir), overlapping the IV insulin infusion for 60 to 120 minutes so basal insulin takes effect. The infusion is then stopped at a meal when a rapid-acting bolus is also given. Ceasing IV insulin without this overlap produces rebound ketosis, and rapid-acting insulin alone cannot substitute for basal cover.
key_points: Resolution: pH > 7.3, HCO3 > 15, ketones < 1 mmol/L, oral tolerating
Give basal SC insulin then overlap IV for 60 to 120 minutes
Never cease IV insulin without overlap or ketosis returns
Time the switch to a meal so rapid-acting cover can begin
explanation.pearls: For a newly diagnosed child, an initial total daily dose of 0.7 to 1.0 units/kg split as 40 to 50 percent basal glargine and the remainder as prandial rapid-acting is a reasonable starting regimen.

options.rationale: AU DKA guidance transitions once pH is above 7.3, bicarbonate above 15 and ketones under 1: give SC basal insulin, continue the IV infusion for at least 60 minutes for basal onset, then stop at a meal.
Ceasing IV insulin before subcutaneous insulin has taken effect leaves an unopposed gap that causes rebound ketosis; overlap between IV and SC insulin is required.
Acidosis and ketosis have already resolved; increasing the infusion rate now causes hypoglycaemia and delays her discharge planning without clinical benefit.
Rapid-acting insulin alone does not provide basal cover and nil by mouth removes the carbohydrate that mealtime bolus insulin is intended to cover; basal insulin is required.
Prolonging the infusion after resolution wastes HDU resources, delays education and diet, and offers no clinical benefit once acidosis and ketosis have cleared.

explanation.summary: First relapse of steroid-sensitive nephrotic syndrome is treated with oral prednisolone 60 mg/m2 daily until three consecutive days of urine protein-free, then 40 mg/m2 on alternate days for 4 weeks and stop. Extended 12 week courses are reserved for the initial presentation. Steroid-sparing agents such as cyclophosphamide or calcineurin inhibitors are added only for frequent relapses or steroid dependence.
key_points: First relapse: 60 mg/m2 daily until 3 days protein-free, then 40 mg/m2 alt-day 4 weeks
Initial presentation regimen is longer and should not be re-used
Cyclophosphamide, tacrolimus for frequent relapse or steroid dependence
Biopsy only if steroid-resistant or atypical
explanation.pearls: Steroid dependence is defined as two consecutive relapses during taper or within 14 days of ceasing; frequent-relapsing is 2 relapses in 6 months or 4 in 12 months, either of which prompts steroid-sparing discussion.

sources.label: KDIGO 2021 GN guideline: Nephrotic syndrome in children

options.rationale: This is the initial presentation regimen (extended 12 week course), not the shorter first-relapse regimen used once a child has already had induction therapy.
source_refs: KDIGO 2021 GN guideline: Nephrotic syndrome in children

options.rationale: This is the standard AU first-relapse regimen: daily prednisolone at 60 mg/m2 until 3 consecutive days of protein-free urine, then alternate day 40 mg/m2 for 4 weeks and cease.
source_refs: KDIGO 2021 GN guideline: Nephrotic syndrome in children

options.rationale: Cyclophosphamide is reserved for frequent relapsers or steroid-dependent disease, not for a single first relapse in a previously well-controlled child.
source_refs: KDIGO 2021 GN guideline: Nephrotic syndrome in children

options.rationale: IV methylprednisolone pulses and biopsy are considered for steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome, not a steroid-sensitive first relapse in a child previously responsive to oral steroids.
source_refs: KDIGO 2021 GN guideline: Nephrotic syndrome in children

options.rationale: Calcineurin inhibitors are steroid-sparing agents reserved for frequent-relapsing or steroid-dependent disease, not a first relapse in a previously stable child on prednisolone.
source_refs: KDIGO 2021 GN guideline: Nephrotic syndrome in children

explanation.summary: PGE1 opens and maintains a patent ductus arteriosus in ductal-dependent lesions such as critical coarctation. Higher initial doses of 0.05 to 0.1 microgram/kg/min are used to reopen a closed duct; once patency is confirmed the infusion is titrated to the lowest effective dose of 0.01 to 0.02 microgram/kg/min to minimise apnoea, hypotension and vasodilatation. Intubation before transfer is standard practice.
key_points: Reopen closed duct with 0.05 to 0.1 microgram/kg/min PGE1
Once open, titrate to 0.01 to 0.02 microgram/kg/min lowest effective dose
Apnoea, hypotension, fever and flushing are dose-related side effects
Intubate before retrieval; do not rely on caffeine or CPAP alone
explanation.pearls: In critical coarctation, aim for pre-ductal SpO2 around 75 to 85 percent to balance Qp and Qs; higher pre-ductal SpO2 risks systemic hypoperfusion from pulmonary steal.

sources.label: NETS retrieval guideline: Neonatal cardiac emergencies
eTG complete: Prostaglandin E1 in ductal-dependent lesions

options.rationale: Apnoea from PGE1 requires airway control not dose reduction alone; the duct is only just opening and dose reduction without airway support risks re-closure and unsupported apnoea.
source_refs: NETS retrieval guideline: Neonatal cardiac emergencies

options.rationale: Caffeine has slow onset and does not reliably prevent PGE1-induced apnoea; established apnoea with dropping temperature and rising lactate requires definitive airway control before transport.
source_refs: NETS retrieval guideline: Neonatal cardiac emergencies

options.rationale: PGE1-induced apnoea is expected: once ductal patency and pre and post-ductal oxygenation are confirmed the infusion can be titrated down to the lowest effective dose while the airway is safely controlled by intubation.
source_refs: NETS retrieval guideline: Neonatal cardiac emergencies

options.rationale: Ceasing PGE1 will close the duct and cause immediate collapse in a ductal-dependent lesion; the priority here is airway control and continuing PGE1, not adrenaline.
source_refs: NETS retrieval guideline: Neonatal cardiac emergencies

options.rationale: Higher dose PGE1 increases apnoea, fever and hypotension without additional ductal benefit once patency is achieved; the maintenance dose window is 0.01 to 0.02 microgram/kg/min.
source_refs: NETS retrieval guideline: Neonatal cardiac emergencies

explanation.summary: Term infants with cord pH under 7.00 or base excess more negative than -12 plus moderate or severe encephalopathy within 6 hours of birth qualify for therapeutic hypothermia to a core temperature of 33.5 C for 72 hours. Passive cooling starts locally while awaiting retrieval, avoiding hyperthermia which worsens injury. Seizure control uses phenobarbital as first-line in AU nurseries. Active warming, delay, or fluid boluses are contraindicated in this window.
key_points: Cord pH under 7.00 or BE worse than -12 plus encephalopathy triggers cooling
Cooling window is 6 hours of birth; passive cooling starts locally
Target core temperature 33.5 C for 72 hours via servo control at tertiary NICU
Phenobarbital first-line for neonatal seizures; avoid phenytoin as first-line
explanation.pearls: Sarnat staging distinguishes moderate (stupor, hypotonia, weak suck, seizures) from severe (coma, flaccid, absent brainstem reflexes) encephalopathy; both qualify for cooling but severe carries markedly worse prognosis regardless of therapy.

options.rationale: Normothermia in a term infant who meets HIE cooling criteria worsens outcome; cooling must start within 6 hours of birth and the transfer window is time critical, not routine.
Active warming to 37.5 C in HIE increases neuronal injury and phenytoin is not first-line for neonatal seizures in AU nurseries; the correct step is cooling and retrieval.

Cord pH under 7.00, base excess more negative than -12, encephalopathy and seizures within 6 hours meet AU therapeutic hypothermia criteria; passive cooling starts locally while awaiting retrieval for active servo-controlled whole-body cooling.
Waiting 2 hours for aEEG delays the therapeutic window; encephalopathy grade can be assessed clinically now with Sarnat and the cord gas and seizure already meet cooling criteria.
A fluid bolus is not indicated without hypovolaemia and cooling should not be deferred; volume overload worsens cerebral oedema in HIE and delays a time-critical neuroprotective intervention.

explanation.summary: Monosymptomatic nocturnal enuresis in a child aged 6 or older with no daytime symptoms, normal urinalysis and a motivated family is first-line managed with an enuresis alarm program for at least 8 to 12 weeks. Desmopressin is a second option or short-term bridge for school camps. Anticholinergics are for overactive bladder features. Imaging and urodynamics are reserved for red flags like daytime wetting, recurrent UTI, or neurology.
key_points: Alarm therapy is first-line from age 6 with a motivated family
Desmopressin second-line or short-term for events
Oxybutynin only if daytime OAB features
No imaging or urodynamics unless daytime symptoms or red flags
explanation.pearls: Continue alarm therapy until 14 consecutive dry nights are achieved; stopping earlier predicts relapse. Overlearning by taking extra evening fluid before final dry weeks reduces relapse rates further.

options.rationale: Desmopressin is a second-line or short-term option when the family cannot commit to an alarm; it does not retrain the arousal response and relapse is common on cessation.
Anticholinergics are used for daytime overactive bladder features; this child has no daytime symptoms so a bladder-relaxant adds side effects without benefit.
Uncomplicated monosymptomatic enuresis with normal urinalysis and no red flags does not warrant urodynamics; imaging is reserved for daytime symptoms, recurrent UTIs, or neurology signs.
Lifting and simple reward alone yield lower cure rates than an alarm program; star charts are supportive but not standalone first-line at age 8 in AU pathways.

For monosymptomatic nocturnal enuresis in a motivated child aged 6 years or older, an enuresis alarm program is the AU first-line therapy with the best long-term dry rates, provided the child is motivated and parents can respond overnight.

explanation.summary: Referred knee pain in an overweight adolescent with obligatory external rotation on hip flexion is classical for a slipped upper femoral epiphysis. Diagnosis is confirmed on AP and frog-lateral pelvic X-rays. Management is immediate strict non-weight bearing and urgent orthopaedic referral for in situ percutaneous screw fixation. Delay risks further slip and avascular necrosis of the femoral head.
key_points: Adolescent hip or referred knee pain with external rotation = suspect SUFE
AP and frog-lateral pelvic X-rays are first-line imaging
Immediate strict non-weight bearing until definitive fixation
Definitive treatment is in situ percutaneous screw pinning
explanation.pearls: The contralateral hip develops SUFE in up to 40 percent of cases; unilateral SUFE under age 10 or over age 16 warrants endocrine workup for hypothyroidism, growth hormone deficiency or renal osteodystrophy.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Slipped upper femoral epiphysis

options.rationale: Ambulatory NSAID therapy misses the diagnosis and permits ongoing weight bearing that can progress a stable slip to unstable, dramatically increasing avascular necrosis risk.
source_refs: RCH CPG: Slipped upper femoral epiphysis

options.rationale: The obligatory external rotation on hip flexion in an overweight adolescent is classical for a slipped upper femoral epiphysis, which is a surgical emergency; strict non-weight bearing is essential to prevent further slip and avascular necrosis.
source_refs: RCH CPG: Slipped upper femoral epiphysis

options.rationale: MRI is not the initial modality for suspected SUFE; plain AP and frog-lateral pelvic X-rays are diagnostic and available urgently, and any delay in immobilisation risks progression.
source_refs: RCH CPG: Slipped upper femoral epiphysis

options.rationale: Endocrine workup for SUFE is done later in atypical cases (very young, very underweight); the immediate priority is imaging, non-weight bearing and orthopaedic pinning to prevent further slip.
source_refs: RCH CPG: Slipped upper femoral epiphysis

options.rationale: Osgood-Schlatter presents with tibial tubercle pain, not hip external rotation deformity; misattributing SUFE risks catastrophic progression and femoral head necrosis.
source_refs: RCH CPG: Slipped upper femoral epiphysis

explanation.summary: Intermittent colicky pain with knee-drawing episodes, a palpable sausage-shaped mass and redcurrant jelly stool in an infant aged 6 to 24 months is intussusception until proven otherwise. Abdominal ultrasound is the AU first-line diagnostic modality with a target or doughnut sign. In stable children, air enema reduction succeeds in 80 to 90 percent of ileocolic cases. Signs of peritonitis, perforation, or shock mandate operative reduction.
key_points: Colic + redcurrant stool + sausage-shaped mass = intussusception
Ultrasound is first-line imaging in AU
Air enema reduction succeeds in most stable cases
Operative reduction if peritonitis, perforation or shock
explanation.pearls: Recurrence after air enema reduction occurs in about 10 percent, usually within 48 hours; children are typically observed for a minimum 24 hours after successful non-operative reduction before oral trial and discharge.

options.rationale: Plain films are neither sensitive nor specific for intussusception; a normal X-ray does not exclude it and they delay definitive imaging.
CT delivers significant radiation to an infant and delays reduction; ultrasound is the AU first-line and CT is not required in typical presentations.
The classical triad of colicky pain, redcurrant stool and a palpable mass is a surgical emergency; observation with antiemetics wastes the window before ischaemic bowel develops.

Ultrasound has close to 100 percent sensitivity for ileocolic intussusception in experienced hands and is the AU first-line diagnostic step, allowing air enema reduction to be planned rapidly in stable children.
Direct-to-theatre bypasses non-operative air enema reduction, which is successful in 80 to 90 percent of stable ileocolic cases and avoids anaesthesia and surgery in most.

explanation.summary: Any jaundice beyond 2 weeks of age (3 weeks if breastfed) requires a split bilirubin. Conjugated bilirubin above 20 percent of total or above 20 micromol/L is always pathological and biliary atresia is the do-not-miss diagnosis. Kasai portoenterostomy before 60 days of life offers the best chance of native liver survival, so referral is same-day to a paediatric hepatology unit. Pale stools and dark urine strongly support obstructive cholestasis.
key_points: Prolonged jaundice past 2 weeks needs a split bilirubin
Conjugated fraction above 20 percent or 20 micromol/L is pathological
Pale stools + dark urine = obstructive cholestasis pattern
Kasai before 60 days maximises native liver survival
explanation.pearls: Time to Kasai is the strongest modifiable prognostic factor: 10-year native liver survival is around 50 percent when performed before 60 days but drops to under 20 percent when performed after 90 days.

options.rationale: Conjugated bilirubin above 20 percent of total or above 20 micromol/L in a jaundiced infant beyond 2 weeks is biliary atresia until proven otherwise; Kasai portoenterostomy before 60 days of life dramatically improves outcomes.
Breast milk jaundice is unconjugated; conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia is always pathological and demands urgent workup, and the infant is formula fed.

Phototherapy treats unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia and is contraindicated in conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia where it may cause bronze-baby syndrome; the priority is diagnostic referral, not phototherapy.
Ursodeoxycholic acid may be adjunctive but does not treat biliary atresia; delaying referral by 4 to 6 weeks pushes the Kasai window and native liver survival falls sharply after 60 days.
Metabolic and TORCH screens are part of the workup but must not delay hepatology referral for biliary atresia; the Kasai window is the driver of urgency here.

explanation.summary: Failure to pass meconium beyond 48 hours with bilious vomiting, abdominal distension and an explosive gush on rectal examination is the classical presentation of Hirschsprung disease. Contrast enema identifies a transition zone from narrow aganglionic distal bowel to dilated proximal ganglionic bowel. Rectal suction biopsy confirms absence of ganglion cells and hypertrophic nerve trunks. Definitive management is a pull-through procedure once the infant is stable.
key_points: Delayed meconium past 48 hours plus bilious vomiting warrants urgent workup
Explosive gush on rectal exam is highly suggestive of Hirschsprung
Contrast enema identifies transition zone
Suction rectal biopsy is diagnostic gold standard in AU
explanation.pearls: Enterocolitis is the major early complication of untreated Hirschsprung, with fever, distension and bloody diarrhoea; it carries mortality up to 20 percent even after surgical correction and mandates aggressive resuscitation with rectal washouts, IV antibiotics and surgical review.

options.rationale: Sweat testing is used for meconium ileus workup but is age dependent and does not explain the classical explosive gush; Hirschsprung is more likely and time critical.
Empirical enema may temporarily decompress but risks delaying diagnosis of Hirschsprung and does not address the underlying aganglionic segment that mandates surgical planning.

The delayed meconium, bilious vomiting, distension and explosive gush on rectal examination are classical for Hirschsprung disease; contrast enema shows a transition zone and rectal suction biopsy is the AU diagnostic standard.

Malrotation is important to consider with bilious vomiting but the transition-zone pattern on abdominal X-ray and rectal exam findings point to lower obstruction; lower contrast study is the correct next step.
Anorectal manometry has poor accuracy in the neonatal period due to immaturity and is not the initial diagnostic step in AU; contrast enema and rectal biopsy are standard.

explanation.summary: A vomiting, dehydrated male infant in the second week of life with hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and hypoglycaemia has salt-losing congenital adrenal hyperplasia until proven otherwise. Virilisation of the external genitalia and hyperpigmentation support the diagnosis. Immediate management is IV hydrocortisone plus normal saline with dextrose plus calcium gluconate for cardiac protection against hyperkalaemia. Hartmann solution and insulin are contraindicated respectively due to potassium content and hypoglycaemia risk.
key_points: Sodium low, potassium high, glucose low in week 2 infant equals CAH crisis
Hydrocortisone stress dose is definitive treatment
Normal saline with dextrose - not Hartmann - for resuscitation
Calcium gluconate cardioprotection when K above 7 mmol/L
explanation.pearls: 21-hydroxylase deficiency accounts for approximately 95 percent of CAH and salt-losing crisis typically presents in the second week when maternal cortisol has waned; save serum for 17-hydroxyprogesterone and renin before giving hydrocortisone if the sample can be taken without any delay to treatment.

options.rationale: Hartmann contains potassium and worsens the hyperkalaemia in a salt-losing CAH crisis, and sepsis workup alone misses the definitive adrenal replacement that is life-saving.
Furosemide worsens hypovolaemia in a shocked infant and does not treat the mineralocorticoid deficiency; hydrocortisone plus volume plus calcium is the correct initial bundle.
Dexamethasone has no mineralocorticoid activity and hydrocortisone at stress doses covers both requirements; the future stimulation test can still be performed after hydrocortisone if needed.
Insulin risks profound iatrogenic hypoglycaemia in an already hypoglycaemic infant; the priority is hydrocortisone, saline resuscitation, dextrose and calcium for cardiac protection.

This is a salt-losing CAH crisis: hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia and shock in a virilised infant; parenteral hydrocortisone plus fluid, glucose and calcium for hyperkalaemia is immediately life-saving before any biochemical confirmation.

explanation.summary: A cyanotic newborn with a failed hyperoxia test (post-oxygen pre-ductal SpO2 remains under 85 percent), narrow mediastinum, egg-on-side cardiac silhouette and single S2 has transposition of the great arteries until proven otherwise. Immediate management is PGE1 infusion to maintain ductal mixing, intubation for retrieval and urgent transfer for balloon atrial septostomy. Definitive repair is the arterial switch operation in the first 2 weeks of life.
key_points: Failed hyperoxia (post-O2 SpO2 <85%) plus egg-on-side XR equals TGA
PGE1 maintains ductal mixing and is life-saving
Balloon atrial septostomy improves mixing before arterial switch
Definitive: arterial switch in first 2 weeks of life
explanation.pearls: PGE1 is contraindicated in obstructed total anomalous pulmonary venous return because opening the duct increases pulmonary blood flow into an obstructed drainage pathway; that lesion is the one cyanotic newborn where PGE1 causes harm and it requires immediate surgical repair.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Cyanotic congenital heart disease

options.rationale: PPHN in this classical XRay pattern is very unusual and inhaled NO alone will not improve TGA saturations without mixing; failure to give PGE1 would allow ductal closure and death.
source_refs: RCH CPG: Cyanotic congenital heart disease

options.rationale: Obstructed TAPVR shows a small heart with pulmonary oedema, not an egg-on-side silhouette; and PGE1 may worsen obstructed TAPVR by opening the duct further, so is contraindicated.
source_refs: RCH CPG: Cyanotic congenital heart disease

options.rationale: Tetralogy typically presents later with a systolic murmur and boot-shaped heart, not egg-on-side; and hypercyanotic spells occur beyond the first weeks, not the first hours.
source_refs: RCH CPG: Cyanotic congenital heart disease

options.rationale: The egg-on-side silhouette, narrow mediastinum, minimal hyperoxia response and single S2 in a well-perfused cyanotic newborn are classical TGA; PGE1 maintains ductal mixing and balloon atrial septostomy is the definitive rescue.
source_refs: RCH CPG: Cyanotic congenital heart disease

options.rationale: Coarctation would show absent or delayed femoral pulses and preductal-postductal SpO2 differential, not egg-on-side; hyperoxia response is usually better and cyanosis is not the dominant presentation.
source_refs: RCH CPG: Cyanotic congenital heart disease

explanation.summary: This child fulfils fever plus four of five classic Kawasaki criteria on day five, with laboratory features (thrombocytosis, hypoalbuminaemia, sterile pyuria, transaminitis) that raise the pre-test probability further. IVIG 2 g/kg within 10 days of fever onset is the coronary-protective intervention. High-dose aspirin is added for anti-inflammatory effect. A baseline echocardiogram is performed on admission.
key_points: Fever 5+ days plus 4/5 principal criteria diagnoses Kawasaki (incomplete Kawasaki uses labs)
IVIG 2 g/kg single infusion within 10 days reduces aneurysm risk from ~25% to ~4%
High-dose aspirin 30-50 mg/kg/day until afebrile then 3-5 mg/kg antiplatelet dose
Baseline echocardiogram on diagnosis; repeat at 2 and 6 weeks
explanation.pearls: IVIG dose 2 g/kg over 10-12 hours as one infusion; if fever persists 36 hours after infusion, repeat IVIG plus consider methylprednisolone or infliximab.

options.rationale: The child meets classic Kawasaki disease criteria: fever four days or more plus at least four of five principal features (bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis, oropharyngeal changes with strawberry tongue and cracked lips, extremity changes with firm swelling, polymorphous rash, cervical lymphadenopathy >1.5 cm). Sterile pyuria, hypoalbuminaemia, thrombocytosis after day 7 and the inflamed BCG scar support the diagnosis. Australian and RCH guidance is IVIG 2 g/kg as a single infusion within 10 days of fever onset to reduce coronary aneurysm risk from ~25% to ~4%, plus aspirin at anti-inflammatory doses (30-50 mg/kg/day) until afebrile for 48-72 hours then low-dose antiplatelet. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

SSSS causes generalised superficial desquamation with a positive Nikolsky sign and painful skin, not conjunctivitis with strawberry tongue and extremity oedema. Blood cultures would not be first-line here and flucloxacillin does not address the vasculitis. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

Scarlet fever from group A streptococcus can share the strawberry tongue and rash but presents with painful pharyngitis, exudative tonsils, and a sandpaper rash rather than five days of fever with bilateral conjunctivitis and extremity oedema.
