Kawasaki disease requires urgent IVIG within the 10-day treatment window. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

Isolated cervical adenitis does not explain the multi-system findings and rash. Antibiotic monotherapy for a suspected bacterial neck infection would miss the diagnosis and delay coronary-protective IVIG. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

Five days of fever with bilateral non-exudative conjunctivitis, oral changes, extremity oedema, polymorphous rash and cervical adenopathy fulfil Kawasaki criteria and mandate hospital treatment. Missing the window increases coronary aneurysm risk substantially. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

explanation.summary: RCH bronchiolitis pathway uses low-flow nasal prong 1 to 2 L/min as first-line oxygen with SpO2 target of 90% or above. Escalation to HFNC is reserved for treatment failure at 1 to 2 hours defined by hypoxia despite low-flow, increasing work of breathing or rising respiratory rate. Bronchodilators, steroids and antibiotics are not routinely indicated. Feeding assessment guides transition to nasogastric feeds.
key_points: SpO2 target 90% (not 92-94%) for bronchiolitis under 12 months per RCH
Low-flow nasal prong 1-2 L/min is first-line oxygen; HFNC only for low-flow failure at 1-2 hours
Bronchodilators, corticosteroids and adrenaline nebulisers not routinely recommended
NGT feeds if intake <50% of maintenance or moderate/severe work of breathing
explanation.pearls: Do not use HFNC as a first-line escalation. RCH audit found 32% of HFNC starts were premature; low-flow held saturations in 68%.

options.rationale: RCH bronchiolitis guidance reserves HFNC for infants who fail to improve on low-flow oxygen after 1 to 2 hours, defined as persistent hypoxia despite low-flow, worsening work of breathing, or increasing respiratory rate. This infant is stable on low-flow with SpO2 within the acceptable target range and improving respiratory rate, so premature escalation adds no benefit while consuming a scarce resource. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

RCH bronchiolitis guidance targets SpO2 90% or above, uses nasal prong 1 to 2 L/min as first-line oxygen, and formally reassesses at 1 to 2 hours. This infant has met target saturation, respiratory rate is trending down, work of breathing is mild, and enteral feeding is tolerated. Continuing the current plan and reassessing is the correct action. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

Bronchodilators are not recommended for bronchiolitis under 12 months. AAP and RCH advise against routine salbutamol, which does not improve length of stay, oxygen requirement, or admission rate in bronchiolitis. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

NGT feeding is indicated for bronchiolitis when work of breathing is moderate to severe, respiratory rate exceeds 60 sustained on oxygen, oral intake drops below 50% of maintenance, or the infant cannot coordinate suck and breath. This infant just took a full feed volume and has improving work of breathing. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

The infant is only 2.5 hours into oxygen therapy and remains on 1 L/min to hold SpO2 at 90%. Trials off oxygen are typically considered after sustained SpO2 above 92% on minimal supplemental oxygen with settled work of breathing, usually the following morning. Weaning now is premature. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

explanation.summary: The at-risk term infant with asymptomatic hypoglycaemia between 1.5 and 2.5 mmol/L should receive 40% dextrose buccal gel 200 mg/kg with an immediate feed. The Sugar Babies protocol reduces NICU admissions and preserves breastfeeding. Symptomatic infants or those with blood glucose below 1.5 mmol/L go straight to IV dextrose bolus.
key_points: Blood glucose <2.6 mmol/L in at-risk infants (IDM, LGA, SGA, preterm) triggers action
Asymptomatic 1.5-2.5 mmol/L: 40% dextrose gel 200 mg/kg (0.5 mL/kg) buccal plus feed
Symptomatic OR <1.5 mmol/L: 10% dextrose IV bolus 2 mL/kg then infusion 60 mL/kg/day
Recheck glucose 30 minutes after feed following gel
explanation.pearls: Buccal 40% dextrose gel dose is 200 mg/kg = 0.5 mL/kg; maximum two doses in 24 hours before escalating to IV.

options.rationale: Neonatal blood glucose below 2.6 mmol/L in an at-risk infant requires action, not observation. The infant of a diabetic mother and a large-for-gestational-age infant are both listed at-risk groups by RCH and the ADIPS/NICE-derived Australian pathway. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal hypoglycaemia)

IV dextrose bolus 2 mL/kg of 10% dextrose is reserved for symptomatic hypoglycaemia (jitteriness, seizures, apnoea, poor tone) or blood glucose persistently below 1.5 mmol/L despite feeds and buccal dextrose gel. This asymptomatic infant with a modestly low reading warrants a staged feed-and-gel approach first. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal hypoglycaemia)

For asymptomatic infants in an at-risk category with blood glucose 1.5 to 2.5 mmol/L, RCH and the Sugar Babies trial pathway recommend 40% dextrose gel 200 mg/kg (0.5 mL/kg) massaged into the buccal mucosa with an immediate feed, followed by a repeat blood glucose 30 minutes after the feed. This halves the rate of admission for IV dextrose. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal hypoglycaemia)

Interrupting breastfeeding removes the strongest driver of postnatal glucose stabilisation. Buccal gel plus continued direct breastfeeding is preferred; NGT feeds are reserved for infants unable to feed effectively at the breast or bottle. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal hypoglycaemia)

Point-of-care meters are known to be less accurate at extreme lows, but pathway guidance is to act on the bedside reading in a well infant while a paired sample is being processed, because delayed treatment risks neurological injury if the true glucose is low. Confirmatory sampling is drawn at the same time, not awaited before intervention. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal hypoglycaemia)

explanation.summary: Refractory anaphylaxis after two doses of IM adrenaline requires escalation to IV adrenaline infusion and adjunctive volume resuscitation. Beta-blocker-treated patients may fail to respond to adrenaline, and glucagon (1 to 5 mg IV in adults; 20 to 30 microgram/kg to a max 1 mg in children) bypasses beta-adrenergic blockade via direct activation of cardiac cAMP. All patients require observation for at least 4 hours after resolution because of biphasic reaction risk.
key_points: IM adrenaline 10 mcg/kg (max 500 mcg) via ASCIA banded table is first-line; repeat every 5 min
Refractory shock or stridor: IV adrenaline infusion 0.05-0.1 mcg/kg/min titrated to response
IV crystalloid 20 mL/kg bolus for hypotension, repeat as needed
Beta-blocked refractory anaphylaxis: glucagon 20-30 mcg/kg IV (max 1 mg) then infusion 5-15 mcg/min in adults
explanation.pearls: ASCIA EpiPen banded table: 150 mcg for 7.5-20 kg (EpiPen Jr), 300 mcg for 20+ kg (EpiPen); never use 10 mcg/kg arithmetic in a real event.

options.rationale: Corticosteroids are adjunctive and do not treat immediate airway or circulatory compromise. Onset is delayed by hours and they have no role as second-line management of acute anaphylaxis with persistent hypotension. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines)

Antihistamines relieve urticaria and itch but have no effect on airway obstruction or hypotension. They are not first- or second-line in refractory anaphylaxis and should never delay adrenaline infusion or fluids. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines)

In refractory anaphylaxis after two IM doses, ASCIA guidance is to move to IV adrenaline infusion titrated to response (start 0.1 microgram/kg/min), give a 20 mL/kg saline bolus for hypotension, and specifically in patients on beta-blockade with refractory hypotension consider glucagon 1 to 5 mg IV (paediatric 20 to 30 microgram/kg to a maximum of 1 mg) followed by infusion because glucagon bypasses beta-adrenergic blockade via cAMP. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines)

Nebulised salbutamol may help wheeze but does not address stridor, laryngeal oedema or hypotension. Adrenaline remains the definitive agent for anaphylactic airway and circulatory compromise. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines)

Definitive airway is escalated when medical management fails to reverse laryngeal oedema and the airway is becoming unsustainable. Cricothyroidotomy is a last-resort rescue after failure of medical therapy and attempted intubation, not the immediate next step while pharmacological options remain available. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Fluoxetine is the first-line SSRI for adolescent major depressive disorder failing an adequate trial of evidence-based psychological therapy such as CBT or IPT-A. TADS demonstrated combination of fluoxetine plus CBT is more effective than either alone. Weekly monitoring for treatment-emergent suicidal ideation is mandated for at least 4 weeks after starting. Full antidepressant effect is assessed at 4 to 6 weeks.
key_points: Adolescent MDD first-line pharmacotherapy: fluoxetine 10 mg titrated to 20 mg
Combine with evidence-based CBT or IPT-A (superiority over either alone in TADS)
Weekly monitoring for suicidal ideation for first 4-6 weeks after starting SSRI
Sertraline is second-line adolescent SSRI; escitalopram third-line specialist choice
explanation.pearls: TADS trial: fluoxetine + CBT 71% response, fluoxetine alone 61%, CBT alone 43%, placebo 35% at 12 weeks. Combination is preferred whenever both are available.

options.rationale: Citalopram is not first-line for adolescent depression in Australia. RANZCP guidance and TGA-approved indications point to fluoxetine as the first-line SSRI with the strongest paediatric evidence base and TGA approval for use in this age group. (Source: RANZCP Depression in Youth)

Sertraline is used as second-line in adolescents when fluoxetine has failed or is not tolerated. Fluoxetine is preferred first-line because of the strongest paediatric RCT evidence (TADS) and TGA registration. (Source: RANZCP Depression in Youth)

Venlafaxine is not first-line in adolescents because of higher rates of hypertension, discontinuation symptoms and increased signal for suicidal ideation in paediatric RCTs. It is reserved for treatment-resistant cases with specialist supervision. (Source: RANZCP Depression in Youth)

Fluoxetine is the first-line SSRI for adolescent moderate-severe major depressive disorder after failure of an adequate psychological therapy trial. TADS demonstrated superiority of fluoxetine plus CBT over either alone and TGA registration supports use in this age group. Starting at 10 mg daily and titrating to 20 mg after 1 to 2 weeks reduces initial activation. Weekly monitoring for suicidal ideation is required in the first 4 to 6 weeks per RANZCP guidance. (Source: RANZCP Depression in Youth)

Mirtazapine has limited paediatric RCT data and is not endorsed as first-line in adolescents. Weight-gain and sedation side-effect profile also disfavours it in an adolescent with existing weight loss where activation is desired. (Source: RANZCP Depression in Youth)

explanation.summary: Bruising in a non-mobile infant, torso and head site bruising, and long-bone fracture with a history inconsistent with the child's developmental stage are strong indicators of inflicted injury. Immediate steps are admission for a safe environment, mandatory statutory notification to the state child protection service by any doctor, and a comprehensive investigation cascade (full skeletal survey, non-contrast CT head, dilated ophthalmology for retinal haemorrhage). Alternative explanations are investigated in parallel, not before, safeguarding.
key_points: TEN-4 FACESp bruising rule: bruises to torso, ear, neck under 4 years or any bruise in infant <4 months warrants NAI evaluation
Full skeletal survey mandatory in <2 years with suspected inflicted injury
Non-contrast CT head and dilated ophthalmology exam to detect occult subdural + retinal haemorrhages
Mandatory reporter notification is a legal duty; not dependent on caseworker approval
explanation.pearls: Fractures with high specificity for inflicted injury include metaphyseal corner (classic metaphyseal lesion), posterior rib, scapular, spinous process and sternal fractures.

options.rationale: The pattern here (bruising in a non-mobile infant, torso and head sites, and a long-bone spiral fracture with a history discordant with the child's developmental stage) meets multiple red flags for inflicted injury. Discharging without paediatric admission, safeguarding involvement and full skeletal survey would fail the child. (Source: RCH CPG: Child Abuse)

While metabolic and skeletal disorders (osteogenesis imperfecta, copper deficiency) are on the differential, they are investigated in parallel with, not before, mandatory child protection notification and admission. The child's protection cannot wait for a genetic workup. (Source: RCH CPG: Child Abuse)

Discharge home is unsafe when inflicted injury is suspected. The child requires medical admission for full evaluation, protective placement decisions and clarity around safe custody. (Source: RCH CPG: Child Abuse)

Confronting either parent alone in the emergency department without a structured multidisciplinary approach can compromise the child's safety, the investigation, and the parent's rights. Assessment is done in a structured setting through the child protection service. (Source: RCH CPG: Child Abuse)

This infant has multiple red flags for inflicted injury: bruising in a pre-mobile infant, high-risk anatomical sites (torso, ears, head), a long-bone fracture at an age when the child cannot yet self-mobilise, and a history discordant with developmental stage. Australian and RCH guidance mandates admission, statutory notification to the state child protection service by any doctor as a mandatory reporter, and a full skeletal survey in infants under 2 years, with non-contrast CT head and dilated ophthalmology examination to look for occult subdural haemorrhage and retinal haemorrhages. (Source: RCH CPG: Child Abuse)

explanation.summary: A term neonate with a focal seizure and normal blood glucose requires urgent transfer to a special care nursery for broad workup: full septic screen including lumbar puncture, empirical antibiotics plus aciclovir for HSV encephalitis, urgent EEG, cranial imaging (ultrasound then MRI), metabolic panel including plasma amino acids, ammonia, lactate, acylcarnitine profile and a pyridoxine trial. First-line anticonvulsant for recurrent seizure is phenobarbital 20 mg/kg IV. Family history of self-limited familial neonatal epilepsy is a diagnosis of exclusion after infection, structural and metabolic causes are excluded.
key_points: Neonatal seizure with normal BSL: broad workup including septic screen with LP, empirical Abx + aciclovir, EEG, MRI, metabolic panel including pyridoxine trial
First-line acute anticonvulsant: phenobarbital 20 mg/kg IV; second-line phenytoin 20 mg/kg IV
HSV encephalitis in neonate can present with focal seizure without skin lesions; empirical aciclovir is mandatory until PCR back
Self-limited familial neonatal epilepsy (KCNQ2) is a diagnosis of exclusion; suspicion warrants genetic panel
explanation.pearls: Pyridoxine-dependent seizure responds to 100 mg IV pyridoxine given during EEG-monitored administration; presence of seizure cessation is diagnostic and requires life-long supplementation.

options.rationale: Oral phenytoin absorption in neonates is erratic and phenytoin is not first-line for neonatal seizure. Discharge to routine observation misses the essential workup for infection and structural cause. (Source: RCH CPG Neonatal seizures)

This event is not consistent with benign neonatal jitteriness: jitteriness is stimulus-sensitive, stoppable with limb hold, and lacks eye deviation, apnoea and postictal drowsiness. The presentation is a focal clonic seizure requiring urgent workup. (Source: RCH CPG Neonatal seizures)

Vitamin K is important for haemostasis but does not treat or diagnose neonatal seizure. Deferring workup means missing time-critical causes such as meningitis or hypoglycaemia recurrence. (Source: RCH CPG Neonatal seizures)

A term neonate with a focal clonic seizure of this description and a family history of self-limited familial neonatal epilepsy (KCNQ2 phenotype) requires broad emergency workup because early identification of infection (bacterial meningitis, HSV encephalitis), stroke, structural brain lesion, and inborn errors of metabolism (pyridoxine-dependent seizure, urea cycle defect) is time-critical. RCH and PSANZ neonatal seizure guidance mandate full septic screen with lumbar puncture, empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics plus aciclovir, EEG, cranial imaging and metabolic workup including a pyridoxine trial. First-line acute anticonvulsant is phenobarbital 20 mg/kg IV. (Source: RCH CPG Neonatal seizures)

A single positive family history is not diagnostic and the workup must be broader; anticonvulsant plans, imaging, metabolic testing and cover for HSV encephalitis must accompany the septic workup. Narrow investigation risks missing critical causes. (Source: RCH CPG Neonatal seizures)

explanation.summary: ITP with wet purpura in a child (active mucosal bleeding) and platelets under 20 x10^9/L is a treatment indication because of the small but serious risk of intracranial haemorrhage. IVIG 0.8 to 1 g/kg is first-line for speed of platelet rise. Dry purpura in a well child with isolated thrombocytopenia may be observed. Bone marrow aspirate is not required if the film is otherwise normal.
key_points: Dry purpura, well child: observe
Wet purpura or platelets <20: treat (IVIG first-line for speed)
Steroid alternative (prednisolone 4 mg/kg/d x 4d) if IVIG contraindicated
Platelet transfusion only for life-threatening bleed as bridge
explanation.pearls: Paediatric ICH risk in ITP is 0.1 to 1%; wet purpura triples risk. Avoid IM injections, NSAIDs, aspirin, and contact sport while count is low.

options.rationale: Observation alone applies to dry purpura (skin bruising and petechiae only) in a well child; active mucosal bleeding (wet purpura) shifts management towards pharmacological intervention due to intracranial bleed risk. (Source: RCH ITP)

Newly diagnosed ITP with wet purpura (mucosal bleeding, epistaxis, gum bleed) plus platelets under 20 x10^9/L warrants urgent platelet elevation; IVIG 0.8 to 1 g/kg gives fastest platelet rise (typically within 24 to 48 h) with a favourable side-effect profile in children. (Source: RCH ITP)

Platelet transfusion in ITP is generally ineffective because transfused platelets are destroyed by autoantibody; reserve for life-threatening bleeding as a bridging measure with immunoglobulin and steroid together. (Source: RCH ITP)

Bone marrow aspirate is not required when the presentation is classic ITP (isolated thrombocytopenia, well child, no atypical features on film); it may be done later only if the response to first-line therapy is atypical. (Source: RCH ITP)

High-dose oral steroid is a valid alternative but is slower to raise platelets than IVIG and requires excluding malignancy on film beforehand; IVIG is preferred in active mucosal bleeding for speed of response. (Source: RCH ITP)

explanation.summary: Cerebral oedema is the leading cause of DKA mortality in children. Risk factors include younger age, severe acidosis at presentation, higher urea, low PaCO2, and treatment with bicarbonate or excess fluid. Warning signs (Muir/Glaser): headache, recurrent vomiting, drowsiness, incontinence, hypertension with bradycardia, cranial nerve palsy, abnormal breathing pattern. Treatment is immediate hyperosmolar therapy (3 percent saline 3 mL/kg over 15 minutes or mannitol 0.5 g/kg over 15 minutes), reduce fluid rate, elevate head, and CT after stabilisation.
key_points: Cushing physiology (hypertension + bradycardia) with headache/vomiting equals cerebral oedema
Treat with 3% saline 3 mL/kg or mannitol 0.5 g/kg IV before CT
Reduce fluid rate by one-third; avoid rapid glucose fall (>5 mmol/L/h)
Avoid bicarbonate; add dextrose when glucose <14 to prevent hypoglycaemia
explanation.pearls: Fluid deficit calculation in paediatric DKA: assume 5 to 7% dehydration in DKA, 10% in HHS; replace over 48 hours plus maintenance. Two-bag system (0.9% saline vs 0.9% saline plus 10% dextrose) allows steady glucose fall.

options.rationale: The concern here is cerebral oedema, not persistent acidosis; increasing insulin without addressing the neurological signs is dangerous. Ongoing rehydration and steady insulin at 0.05 unit/kg/hour is appropriate provided glucose fall is not too fast. (Source: RCH DKA)

Additional aggressive rehydration risks worsening cerebral oedema; total fluid rate should be reduced by one-third when oedema is suspected. Rising BP and falling pulse are Cushing physiology, not hypovolaemia. (Source: RCH DKA)

Bradycardia and rising BP with headache, vomiting and depressed conscious level are Muir/Glaser cerebral oedema criteria requiring immediate hyperosmolar therapy; 3 percent saline 3 mL/kg IV (or mannitol 0.5 g/kg) is first-line before any imaging. (Source: RCH DKA)
Treatment must not be delayed for imaging when cerebral oedema is clinically apparent; hyperosmolar therapy is given first, then CT once stabilised (or if there is no response). (Source: RCH DKA)
Bicarbonate is contraindicated in paediatric DKA except in life-threatening hyperkalaemia because it worsens cerebral oedema and paradoxical CNS acidosis. (Source: RCH DKA)

explanation.summary: Kawasaki disease diagnosis requires 5 or more days of fever plus 4 of 5 principal criteria (bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis, oral mucosal changes, polymorphous rash, peripheral extremity changes, cervical lymphadenopathy). Incomplete Kawasaki is diagnosed with 2 or 3 principal criteria plus supportive laboratory or echocardiographic findings, particularly in infants under 12 months (highest risk group for coronary aneurysms). Treatment is IVIG 2 g/kg plus aspirin, with echocardiography to document coronary status.
key_points: Classic KD: fever >=4 days plus 4 of 5 principal criteria
Incomplete KD: fever >=5 days plus 2 or 3 criteria plus supportive labs
Infants <12 months at highest risk for coronary aneurysms; low threshold to treat
Treatment: IVIG 2 g/kg single dose + aspirin 3 to 5 mg/kg/d (some centres 30 to 80)
explanation.pearls: AHA supportive lab criteria for incomplete KD (at least 3 of): anaemia for age, platelets over 450 after day 7, albumin under 30, ALT elevated, WCC over 15, sterile pyuria. Kobayashi score identifies IVIG-resistant patients for adjunctive steroid.

options.rationale: Steroids are second-line in Kawasaki (used with IVIG in high-risk or IVIG-resistant cases per the Kobayashi score), not first-line monotherapy; IVIG remains the primary therapy. (Source: RCH Kawasaki)
Delaying IVIG beyond day 10 of illness increases coronary artery aneurysm risk; if incomplete Kawasaki criteria are met, treatment should not await further sepsis workup. (Source: RCH Kawasaki)
A well-appearing infant with 6 days of fever and inflammatory picture is unsafe to discharge without excluding Kawasaki disease; missed cases risk coronary aneurysms. (Source: RCH Kawasaki)

Prolonged fever with only two of five principal Kawasaki criteria (rash and non-purulent conjunctivitis) in an infant with supportive laboratory findings (raised CRP, thrombocytosis, hypoalbuminaemia, sterile pyuria, transaminitis, anaemia) meets AHA incomplete Kawasaki criteria; treatment is IVIG 2 g/kg plus aspirin, and echocardiography documents coronary status. (Source: RCH Kawasaki)
Antibiotics alone are insufficient if incomplete Kawasaki criteria are met and delay definitive therapy; concurrent bacterial infection does not exclude Kawasaki disease. (Source: RCH Kawasaki)

explanation.summary: Severe neonatal hyperbilirubinaemia with acute bilirubin encephalopathy is a neurological emergency. Immune haemolytic causes (Rh, ABO, minor blood group incompatibility) have a positive DAT and elevated reticulocyte count. When bilirubin exceeds the exchange transfusion threshold on the age-specific nomogram, or when signs of acute bilirubin encephalopathy appear (lethargy, hypotonia, poor feed, high-pitched cry, opisthotonos, seizures), immediate double-volume exchange transfusion is indicated with concurrent intensive phototherapy. IVIG 0.5 g/kg reduces need for exchange in immune haemolysis.
key_points: Bilirubin above exchange line OR any acute encephalopathy signs equals immediate exchange
IVIG 0.5 g/kg over 2 hours in immune haemolysis may reduce need for exchange
Continue intensive phototherapy throughout
Isovolumetric exchange with double blood volume (~160 mL/kg)
explanation.pearls: NICE and RCH nomograms differ slightly; the current RCH exchange line at 60 hours for a well term baby is roughly 430 micromol/L (lower with haemolysis or prematurity). Escalate immediately if encephalopathy signs present regardless of exact number.

options.rationale: Bilirubin above the exchange transfusion threshold at 60 hours with clinical features of acute bilirubin encephalopathy (lethargy, poor tone, poor cry) mandates immediate exchange, not further observation on phototherapy alone. (Source: RCH Neonatal Jaundice)

Stopping phototherapy allows further bilirubin rise; ursodeoxycholic acid has no role in unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia. Continued intensive phototherapy alongside exchange is standard. (Source: RCH Neonatal Jaundice)

Simple top-up transfusion does not remove circulating bilirubin or antibody; only exchange transfusion clears both and is required at this bilirubin level with encephalopathy. (Source: RCH Neonatal Jaundice)
Phenobarbital has a slow onset (days) and no role in acute severe hyperbilirubinaemia with encephalopathy; immediate mechanical clearance by exchange is required. (Source: RCH Neonatal Jaundice)

Bilirubin over the exchange line at 60 hours with signs of acute bilirubin encephalopathy in a baby with immune haemolysis requires urgent double-volume exchange transfusion; IVIG 0.5 g/kg over 2 hours may reduce need for exchange in immune haemolytic disease. (Source: RCH Neonatal Jaundice)

explanation.summary: IgA vasculitis nephritis presents as haematuria and/or proteinuria in the weeks to months after the acute vasculitic illness. Weekly urinalysis for 6 to 12 months detects it early. Indications for renal biopsy and nephrology referral include nephrotic range proteinuria (uPCR over 200 mg/mmol), impaired renal function, persistent hypertension, or persistent macroscopic haematuria and proteinuria beyond 3 months. Steroid-based induction is standard for significant nephritis, guided by biopsy histology.
key_points: Weekly urinalysis for 6 to 12 months after acute IgA vasculitis
Biopsy triggers: nephrotic proteinuria, reduced GFR, hypertension, persistent haematuria+proteinuria
Empiric steroids often started pending biopsy
Preventive steroids do NOT prevent nephritis (KIGARI trial)
explanation.pearls: ISKDC classification I to VI grades severity by crescents; over 50% crescents or focal segmental glomerulosclerosis has worse prognosis. Renal outcomes are the main long-term determinant, with 1 to 5% risk of ESKD in nephritic cases.

options.rationale: IgA vasculitis nephritis with nephrotic-range proteinuria, hypertension and reduced eGFR requires urgent nephrology referral, renal biopsy for prognostic and treatment classification (Oxford/ISKDC), and empirical steroid therapy is often started pending biopsy result. (Source: RCH IgA Vasculitis)

Nephrotic-range proteinuria with reduced GFR and hypertension in IgA vasculitis nephritis requires renal biopsy and specialist input, not further observation which risks progression. (Source: RCH IgA Vasculitis)

Normal complement and preceding IgA vasculitis do not fit post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis; antibiotics are not indicated and delay appropriate immunosuppression assessment. (Source: RCH IgA Vasculitis)
Dietary measures alone are insufficient for nephritic-nephrotic syndrome with rising creatinine; specialist assessment and biopsy are needed within days, not weeks. (Source: RCH IgA Vasculitis)
ACE inhibitor is a reasonable adjunct but insufficient alone with nephrotic range proteinuria and reduced GFR; biopsy and immunosuppression assessment are the priority. (Source: RCH IgA Vasculitis)

explanation.summary: Retropharyngeal abscess presents in toddlers as fever, sore throat, drooling, muffled voice, neck extension or torticollis, with lateral neck film showing prevertebral widening (over half vertebral body width at C2, over one vertebral body at C6). Management prioritises airway: keep the child calm, escalate to paediatric anaesthetics and ENT, controlled inhalational induction in theatre, then drainage and IV antibiotics.
key_points: Airway first: keep calm, do not agitate, escalate to ENT and paediatric anaesthetics
Controlled inhalational induction in theatre, NOT RSI in ED
Empiric IV ceftriaxone plus clindamycin (or metronidazole) after airway secured
Contrast CT for surgical planning after airway assessment
explanation.pearls: Distinguish from epiglottitis (rapid onset, tripod, drooling, no torticollis) and croup (barking cough, no drooling). Retropharyngeal lateral film sign: prevertebral soft tissue >7 mm at C2 or >14 mm at C6 (or >1x vertebral body width).

options.rationale: Bedside drainage of a paediatric retropharyngeal abscess risks catastrophic airway loss and aspiration; drainage is done in theatre with definitive airway. (Source: RCH Retropharyngeal Abscess)

Cannulation may cause the child to cry and lose the airway; treatment in a compromised paediatric airway starts with keeping the child calm and moving to a controlled theatre environment, then antibiotics and drainage. (Source: RCH Retropharyngeal Abscess)

Retropharyngeal abscess with airway compromise (stridor, muffled voice, drooling, opisthotonos) in a young child requires controlled airway management in theatre with senior ENT and paediatric anaesthetics; distress can precipitate obstruction. Drainage and IV antibiotics follow airway control. (Source: RCH Retropharyngeal Abscess)

Nebulised adrenaline and dexamethasone are for croup, not deep neck space infection; CT is helpful but only after airway assessment in theatre because a child with mild stridor at rest can decompensate on scanner. (Source: RCH Retropharyngeal Abscess)

Emergency intubation of a paediatric distorted airway in ED risks catastrophic failure; the standard is inhalational induction in theatre by paediatric anaesthetics with ENT available for surgical airway backup. (Source: RCH Retropharyngeal Abscess)

explanation.summary: Chronic functional constipation with faecal impaction in children is managed by (1) disimpaction with high-dose oral macrogol (PEG) for 3 to 7 days, (2) maintenance macrogol titrated to soft daily stools continued for at least 2 to 6 months, (3) toileting behavioural strategy (sit after meals, footstool, reward chart), and (4) parent education. Red flags requiring further workup include delayed meconium, failure to thrive, abnormal spine or perianal examination, or onset before 1 month of age.
key_points: Disimpaction: macrogol 1 to 1.5 g/kg/day PO for 3 days (some centres up to 7)
Maintenance: macrogol titrated to soft daily stool for months, not weeks
Toilet behavioural strategy is essential alongside laxatives
Rectal treatments only if oral fails or refused
explanation.pearls: Movicol Junior (macrogol) sachets: 1 to 2 sachets/day maintenance; 4 to 12 sachets/day for disimpaction depending on age. Do not stop maintenance for at least 2 months of regular painless stools then wean slowly to avoid relapse.

options.rationale: Chronic functional constipation with faecal impaction requires disimpaction with high-dose oral macrogol (1 to 1.5 g/kg/day for 3 days) then maintenance dosing titrated to soft daily stools; parent education and behavioural toileting are essential adjuncts. (Source: RCH Constipation)

Hirschsprung disease presents in early infancy with delayed meconium and typically failure to thrive; a well-grown 5-year-old with classic functional constipation history does not warrant biopsy. (Source: RCH Constipation)

Rectal treatments are more distressing for children and less effective than oral macrogol for both disimpaction and maintenance; oral therapy is first-line unless oral is not tolerated. (Source: RCH Constipation)
ACE is reserved for refractory constipation after optimised medical therapy including adequate disimpaction and maintenance macrogol with behavioural support has failed. (Source: RCH Constipation)

Cow milk protein allergy contributes in a small subset (particularly infants) but is not the first-line intervention in a 5-year-old with classic functional constipation; disimpaction and maintenance is standard. (Source: RCH Constipation)

explanation.summary: Neonatal early-onset sepsis is treated empirically with benzylpenicillin (or ampicillin) plus gentamicin after blood cultures, covering GBS, Listeria, E. coli, and other gram negatives. Ceftriaxone is contraindicated in neonates and hypoglycaemia is corrected with 10 percent dextrose 2 mL per kg IV bolus. Lumbar puncture is performed after stabilisation, not before. Duration is 7 to 10 days if bacteraemia proven, longer for meningitis.
key_points: Empirical regimen: benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin IV
Avoid ceftriaxone in neonates (bilirubin displacement, calcium precipitation)
Correct hypoglycaemia with 10% dextrose 2 mL per kg IV
Lumbar puncture after stabilisation, not before, in unstable neonate
explanation.pearls: RCH Melbourne dosing: benzylpenicillin 60 mg per kg IV 12 hourly first week of life, gentamicin 5 mg per kg IV once daily; add IV aciclovir 20 mg per kg 8 hourly if HSV features (vesicles, seizures, hepatitis).

options.rationale: Vancomycin plus meropenem is not first line for early-onset neonatal sepsis; ben-pen plus gent covers GBS, Listeria, and gram negatives adequately for empirical therapy in the first 72 hours. (Source: RCH Melbourne Neonatal Sepsis Guideline)

Australian neonatal early-onset sepsis empirical regimen is benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin; dextrose 10 percent 2 mL per kg IV corrects the hypoglycaemia in this clinically unstable neonate. (Source: RCH Melbourne Neonatal Sepsis Guideline)

Ceftriaxone is avoided in neonates because it displaces bilirubin and precipitates with calcium containing fluids causing lethal reactions; ben-pen plus gent is standard. (Source: RCH Melbourne Neonatal Sepsis Guideline)
Oral therapy is unsafe in a clinically unstable neonate with shock features; IV antibiotics after blood cultures are mandatory. (Source: RCH Melbourne Neonatal Sepsis Guideline)
Cefotaxime alone lacks reliable Listeria cover; ben-pen (or ampicillin) is required in the neonatal empirical regimen. (Source: RCH Melbourne Neonatal Sepsis Guideline)

explanation.summary: Bronchiolitis in infants is treated supportively with oxygen, minimal handling, and feeding support. HFNC is second line after standard oxygen; if the infant tires or CO2 rises, CPAP is next before intubation. Bronchodilators, steroids, adrenaline, hypertonic saline, and antibiotics are not routinely useful. Retrieval to a PICU should be arranged for infants requiring CPAP.
key_points: Escalation ladder: room air, low flow oxygen, HFNC, CPAP, intubation
Bronchodilators and steroids not indicated in bronchiolitis
Antibiotics only if consolidation or clear bacterial coinfection
HFNC typical settings 2 L per kg per minute, capped around 20 L per minute for infants
explanation.pearls: PARIS trial showed HFNC reduces intubation vs standard oxygen in moderate bronchiolitis; escalate to CPAP if HFNC failure, defined as no improvement in RR, HR, work of breathing, or O2 requirement within 1 to 2 hours.

options.rationale: Empirical antibiotics are not indicated in typical viral bronchiolitis without focal consolidation or clear secondary bacterial infection; they do not address respiratory failure. (Source: RCH Melbourne Bronchiolitis Guideline)

Salbutamol, adrenaline, and steroids are not effective in bronchiolitis and are not recommended; delaying escalation to CPAP with these therapies risks respiratory arrest. (Source: RCH Melbourne Bronchiolitis Guideline)

Severe bronchiolitis with impending failure on HFNC (drowsy, rising CO2, poor perfusion) is escalated to CPAP as the next non-invasive step and PICU is consulted for possible intubation; intubation is reserved for CPAP failure. (Source: RCH Melbourne Bronchiolitis Guideline)

Hypertonic saline has not been shown to improve outcomes in bronchiolitis and does not treat impending respiratory failure; escalation of respiratory support is needed. (Source: RCH Melbourne Bronchiolitis Guideline)

Atelectasis on chest X-ray in bronchiolitis is common and does not require drainage; a chest drain is not indicated without a pneumothorax or significant effusion. (Source: RCH Melbourne Bronchiolitis Guideline)

explanation.summary: Salt-losing CAH crisis is treated by immediate IV hydrocortisone (bolus 25 mg then infusion), 10 percent dextrose for hypoglycaemia, and 0.9 percent saline for volume expansion. Blood should be taken for cortisol and 17-hydroxyprogesterone before steroids where possible but treatment should not be delayed. Dexamethasone has no mineralocorticoid activity and is inappropriate. Hyponatraemia in this setting responds to saline plus hydrocortisone, not hypertonic saline.
key_points: Immediate hydrocortisone (25 mg IV bolus neonate) plus dextrose plus saline
Send cortisol and 17-OHP before steroids where possible but do not delay treatment
Dexamethasone inadequate: no mineralocorticoid activity
Fludrocortisone 100 mcg orally daily added once stable for maintenance
explanation.pearls: Classical 21-hydroxylase deficiency: karyotype 46,XX baby girl with virilised external genitalia, salt-losing crisis in second week of life; stress dose hydrocortisone at 100 mg per m2 per day divided 6 hourly (neonate 25 mg IV bolus then 25 mg 6 hourly).

options.rationale: In CAH crisis the hyponatraemia is due to aldosterone deficiency and volume loss, not free water excess; 0.9 percent saline plus hydrocortisone corrects both safely without ODS risk. (Source: RCH Melbourne CAH Guideline)

Hyperkalaemia in CAH crisis is driven by cortisol and aldosterone deficiency; giving cortisol, dextrose, and saline addresses the cause and lowers potassium without cardiac protective agents unless there are ECG changes. (Source: RCH Melbourne CAH Guideline)

Dexamethasone has no mineralocorticoid activity and is inappropriate for salt-losing crisis; hydrocortisone provides both glucocorticoid and, at stress dose, mineralocorticoid coverage. (Source: RCH Melbourne CAH Guideline)

Salt-losing CAH crisis needs immediate parenteral hydrocortisone (bolus then infusion), correction of hypoglycaemia with dextrose 10 percent, and volume expansion with normal saline; potassium falls with these steps and is not initially treated. (Source: RCH Melbourne CAH Guideline)

Delaying hydrocortisone in shocked neonate with virilisation and biochemistry consistent with CAH is unsafe; treat empirically after taking cortisol and 17-OHP samples. (Source: RCH Melbourne CAH Guideline)

explanation.summary: Classic metaphyseal lesions (bucket-handle or corner fractures) in infants are highly specific for inflicted trauma. Management includes admission, mandatory notification to child protection services, full skeletal survey per RANZCR paediatric imaging protocol, ophthalmology examination for retinal haemorrhages, and MDT involvement including social work. Confidentiality is overridden by mandatory reporting duties.
key_points: Classic metaphyseal fracture in an infant is highly specific for NAI
Mandatory notification to child protection: does not require consent
Full skeletal survey per RANZCR paediatric imaging protocol, repeat at 11 to 14 days
Fundoscopy for retinal haemorrhages, consider neuroimaging under 2 years
explanation.pearls: RANZCR paediatric skeletal survey includes AP and lateral skull, chest, abdomen, spine, humeri, forearms, hands, femora, tibiae, and feet; repeat limited survey 11 to 14 days later increases yield by up to 25 percent as callus becomes visible.

options.rationale: Discharging a pre-mobile infant with a highly specific abuse fracture back to an unassessed environment risks further serious harm; admission and notification are mandatory. (Source: RCH Melbourne Child Abuse Guideline)

Classic metaphyseal lesions are highly specific for non-accidental injury in a pre-mobile child and warrant safeguarding assessment; discharge without further work up would fail the child. (Source: RCH Melbourne Child Abuse Guideline)

Mandatory reporting overrides confidentiality when there is reasonable suspicion of child abuse; discussion should be professional and honest but must not delay notification to child protection services. (Source: RCH Melbourne Child Abuse Guideline)

Metabolic workup can be done in parallel but does not delay notification; osteogenesis imperfecta does not typically cause classic metaphyseal fractures, and safeguarding takes priority. (Source: RCH Melbourne Child Abuse Guideline)

A classic metaphyseal fracture in an infant is highly specific for inflicted injury; admission, mandatory notification, skeletal survey per RANZCR protocol, and ophthalmology examination for retinal haemorrhages are standard. (Source: RCH Melbourne Child Abuse Guideline)

explanation.summary: Acute chest syndrome is diagnosed by a new pulmonary infiltrate on chest X-ray plus one of fever, respiratory symptoms, or hypoxia in a patient with sickle cell disease. Management is oxygen, judicious IV fluid, IV antibiotics (cephalosporin plus macrolide), effective analgesia and incentive spirometry to prevent atelectasis, and transfusion. Exchange transfusion is preferred when hypoxia is severe, multilobar, or deteriorating; simple top-up is used for milder cases.
key_points: ACS: new infiltrate plus fever, respiratory symptoms, or hypoxia in SCD
IV cephalosporin plus macrolide, oxygen, incentive spirometry, adequate analgesia
Exchange transfusion for severe ACS (SpO2 under 90, multilobar, deteriorating)
Simple top-up transfusion for milder ACS with Hb below baseline
explanation.pearls: BSH target HbS below 30 percent post exchange, keep total Hb 100 to 110 g/L to avoid hyperviscosity; incentive spirometry every 2 hours reduces ACS progression in vaso-occlusive crises by around 50 percent.

options.rationale: Acute chest syndrome with hypoxia and dropping haemoglobin needs broad antibiotics for atypicals and encapsulated organisms, careful fluid balance, oxygen, and exchange transfusion to lower HbS below 30 percent. Simple top-up transfusion is used only in mild cases. (Source: BSH Sickle Cell Acute Guidelines)
Over-hydration precipitates pulmonary oedema in ACS, oral amoxicillin does not cover atypicals, and hypoxia with falling haemoglobin needs transfusion. (Source: BSH Sickle Cell Acute Guidelines)

Hydroxycarbamide is chronic prophylaxis and does not treat acute chest syndrome; stopping opioids leads to inadequate analgesia and shallow breathing worsening atelectasis. (Source: BSH Sickle Cell Acute Guidelines)

Simple top-up alone in severe ACS with hypoxia and multilobar or clinical deterioration is insufficient; exchange transfusion targeting HbS under 30 percent is preferred in severe disease. (Source: BSH Sickle Cell Acute Guidelines)

Bronchodilators and steroids are not standard for ACS; delaying antibiotics in a febrile hypoxic child with sickle disease risks progression to sepsis and death. (Source: BSH Sickle Cell Acute Guidelines)

explanation.summary: IVIG-resistant Kawasaki disease is treated with a second IVIG dose plus adjunctive corticosteroids (either short pulses of IV methylprednisolone or oral prednisolone taper). Refractory cases can escalate to infliximab or ciclosporin. Giant coronary aneurysms (Z score over 10 or luminal diameter over 8 mm) require therapeutic anticoagulation with warfarin or LMWH plus aspirin, and long term follow up with cardiology.
key_points: IVIG resistance: retreat with IVIG 2 g per kg plus corticosteroids
Third line escalation: infliximab or ciclosporin
Giant aneurysm (Z over 10 or over 8 mm): dual therapy aspirin plus LMWH or warfarin
Coronary events managed medically first, surgery reserved for ischaemia
explanation.pearls: RAISE trial showed adding IV methylprednisolone 2 mg per kg per day to IVIG reduced coronary abnormalities in high risk Japanese cohort; Kobayashi score is validated in Japanese but has lower sensitivity in Western cohorts, so clinical judgement dominates in Australia.

options.rationale: Aspirin monotherapy is inadequate for IVIG-resistant KD with giant aneurysm and thrombus; ongoing inflammation and thrombus need dual escalation. (Source: AHA Kawasaki Statement 2017)

IVIG-resistant Kawasaki disease with giant coronary aneurysm and intraluminal thrombus needs second dose IVIG plus corticosteroids for inflammation control, plus therapeutic anticoagulation for thrombus prevention or treatment. (Source: AHA Kawasaki Statement 2017)
Aspirin is continued in KD for antiplatelet effect on coronary arteries regardless of platelet count; DOACs are not first line in paediatric KD anticoagulation. (Source: AHA Kawasaki Statement 2017)

Infliximab is a second line option after IVIG plus steroids fail; giving it alone without repeat IVIG or steroids and without anticoagulation for the thrombus is inadequate. (Source: AHA Kawasaki Statement 2017)

CABG is reserved for coronary ischaemia or severe stenosis, not first line for giant aneurysm with fresh thrombus in a febrile child; medical intensification with IVIG, steroids, and anticoagulation is standard. (Source: AHA Kawasaki Statement 2017)

explanation.summary: Witnessed choking on nut or organic material followed by persistent unilateral wheeze, reduced air entry, or expiratory air trapping is a strong indication for rigid bronchoscopy under general anaesthetic. Imaging cannot exclude foreign body aspiration, and delaying bronchoscopy risks post obstructive pneumonia and mucosal damage. Blind physiotherapy manoeuvres are unsafe.
key_points: Witnessed choking plus focal signs: rigid bronchoscopy under GA
Expiratory chest X-ray or fluoroscopy shows air trapping on affected side
Normal imaging does not exclude aspiration
Avoid blind back slaps, chest physiotherapy, or upright posturing
explanation.pearls: Peanut is the most commonly aspirated organic foreign body under 3 years; right main bronchus is more commonly involved due to more vertical anatomy; ventilation lung scan can localise atypical cases if X-ray is normal.

sources.label: RCH Melbourne Foreign Body Aspiration Guideline

options.rationale: Blind physiotherapy manoeuvres can dislodge the foreign body into the trachea causing complete airway obstruction; bronchoscopy is definitive management for suspected lodged aspiration. (Source: RCH Melbourne Foreign Body Aspiration Guideline)
source_refs: RCH Melbourne Foreign Body Aspiration Guideline

options.rationale: Bronchodilators do not remove a foreign body; discharging a child with likely retained peanut risks pneumonia, post obstructive collapse, and migration. (Source: RCH Melbourne Foreign Body Aspiration Guideline)
source_refs: RCH Melbourne Foreign Body Aspiration Guideline

options.rationale: Witnessed choking episode with peanut and persistent unilateral wheeze plus expiratory air trapping is highly suggestive of a lodged organic foreign body; rigid bronchoscopy under GA is the definitive diagnostic and therapeutic procedure. (Source: RCH Melbourne Foreign Body Aspiration Guideline)
source_refs: RCH Melbourne Foreign Body Aspiration Guideline

options.rationale: Antibiotics without removal do not treat the mechanical cause of air trapping and delay bronchoscopic extraction, increasing complication risk. (Source: RCH Melbourne Foreign Body Aspiration Guideline)
source_refs: RCH Melbourne Foreign Body Aspiration Guideline

options.rationale: CT is not required before bronchoscopy when history and expiratory hyperinflation strongly suggest aspiration; it adds radiation, delay, and may not visualise organic material well. (Source: RCH Melbourne Foreign Body Aspiration Guideline)
source_refs: RCH Melbourne Foreign Body Aspiration Guideline

explanation.summary: Severe croup with stridor at rest, marked recession, or hypoxia is treated with nebulised adrenaline and dexamethasone. Minimise handling to avoid worsening obstruction. Anaesthetic and ENT standby is essential in impending failure. Bronchodilators have no role and epiglottitis is rare in immunised children. IV access in a distressed child should be delayed until the airway is secured or improving.
key_points: Severe croup: nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000 solution
Dexamethasone 0.6 mg per kg oral (max 12 mg) or IM if unable to swallow
Minimise handling, no unnecessary investigations, ENT plus anaesthetics standby
Salbutamol and antibiotics not indicated in typical viral croup
explanation.pearls: RCH Melbourne uses dexamethasone 0.6 mg per kg oral (up to 12 mg) as first line; prednisolone 1 mg per kg per day for 3 days is an alternative but with slightly higher relapse rate; observation for at least 3 to 4 hours after adrenaline to detect rebound.

options.rationale: Salbutamol has no role in croup because obstruction is subglottic oedema, not bronchospasm; steroids are the cornerstone therapy. (Source: RCH Melbourne Croup Guideline)

Barking cough with viral prodrome is classic croup, not epiglottitis; distressing the child for X-ray in impending obstruction can precipitate complete airway loss. (Source: RCH Melbourne Croup Guideline)

Severe croup with stridor at rest needs nebulised adrenaline immediately for airway oedema; oral prednisolone alone acts too slowly and observation risks obstruction. (Source: RCH Melbourne Croup Guideline)

Severe croup with stridor at rest and marked recession is treated with nebulised adrenaline for immediate airway oedema relief, corticosteroids (dexamethasone) for sustained benefit, minimal handling to avoid distress, and anaesthetic and ENT standby for intubation if needed. (Source: RCH Melbourne Croup Guideline)

Distressing the child with IV access in impending obstruction can precipitate airway loss; oral or IM dexamethasone and nebulised adrenaline are preferred first steps. (Source: RCH Melbourne Croup Guideline)

explanation.summary: Complete Kawasaki disease is diagnosed on fever of 4 days or more plus at least 4 of 5 principal features (bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis, mucous membrane changes, polymorphous rash, extremity changes, cervical lymphadenopathy). IVIG 2 g/kg plus high-dose aspirin within the first 10 days reduces coronary aneurysm risk from around 25 percent to under 5 percent. Sterile pyuria, transaminitis, and hyponatraemia support the diagnosis. Coronary artery involvement can develop after initial normal echocardiography, so treatment is not withheld while awaiting imaging change.
key_points: IVIG 2 g/kg over 10 hours plus aspirin 30-50 mg/kg/day divided
Treat within 10 days of fever onset; earlier is better
Normal initial echo does not exclude Kawasaki nor delay IVIG
Sterile pyuria supports Kawasaki, not UTI
explanation.pearls: Kobayashi score >=5 flags IVIG-resistance risk and prompts adjunctive IV methylprednisolone 30 mg/kg with the first IVIG dose; refractory fever 36 hours after IVIG triggers second-dose IVIG plus consideration of infliximab.

options.rationale: Delayed IVIG beyond day 10 substantially increases coronary aneurysm risk; complete clinical criteria on day 5 with raised inflammatory markers meet treatment threshold without further delay. (Source: RCH Melbourne Kawasaki Disease Guideline)

Steroid monotherapy is reserved for high-risk features (Kobayashi score) as adjunct to IVIG or for IVIG-resistant disease; it is not first-line alone. (Source: RCH Melbourne Kawasaki Disease Guideline)

Sterile pyuria and prolonged fever are classic Kawasaki features and not indications for empirical antibiotics; LP is not required and would delay definitive therapy. (Source: RCH Melbourne Kawasaki Disease Guideline)

Complete criteria (fever plus at least 4 of 5 principal features) on day 5 with raised CRP indicates prompt IVIG 2 g/kg with high-dose aspirin (30-50 mg/kg/day divided) until afebrile 48 hours, then low-dose aspirin. (Source: RCH Melbourne Kawasaki Disease Guideline)
Oral prednisolone alone is not first-line; delaying IVIG allows continued vasculitis and increases coronary aneurysm risk. (Source: RCH Melbourne Kawasaki Disease Guideline)

explanation.summary: Anaphylaxis with hypotension, airway oedema, and respiratory compromise is a time-critical intervention. IM adrenaline into the anterolateral thigh at ASCIA banded doses (150 mcg for 7.5-20 kg, 300 mcg for over 20 kg) is first-line and can be repeated every 5 minutes. Do not delay the first IM dose to gain IV access. IV adrenaline infusion is reserved for refractory shock in a monitored setting.
key_points: ASCIA banded IM adrenaline: 150 mcg (7.5-20 kg), 300 mcg (>20 kg)
Anterolateral thigh, repeat every 5 min if inadequate response
Give supine with legs elevated unless respiratory distress precludes
Antihistamines and steroids are adjuncts, not primary treatment
explanation.pearls: Biphasic reactions occur in around 5 percent of paediatric anaphylaxis, usually within 4-8 hours; ASCIA advises minimum 4 hours observation after last dose, longer if repeated adrenaline was needed or severe features present.

options.rationale: ASCIA uses banded IM adrenaline doses to avoid arithmetic under pressure; 10 mcg/kg calculation is IV emergency dosing and is not first-line IM in a child collapsed at the roadside. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines)

EpiPen Jr 150 mcg is for 7.5-20 kg per ASCIA but the child is 18 kg with hypotension; the adult 300 mcg dose is preferred at borderline weight with shock, and anterolateral thigh is preferred over deltoid. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines)

ASCIA-banded IM adrenaline for 20 kg or under 6 years is 300 mcg (EpiPen dose); anterolateral thigh gives fastest absorption and can be repeated every 5 min while preparing IV access. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines)

Nebulised adrenaline is adjunct for upper airway oedema (croup or laryngeal angioedema); it does not treat shock or systemic anaphylaxis and delaying IM adrenaline while gaining IV access is unsafe. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines)

IV adrenaline boluses are for arrest or refractory shock only and carry arrhythmia risk; delaying immediate IM adrenaline to gain IV access in a child with progressing airway swelling is unsafe. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Neonatal phototherapy thresholds are age (in hours) and risk-factor dependent. RCH Melbourne charts use a lower risk-factor line for babies with haemolysis (positive DAT or G6PD deficiency), sepsis, prematurity, temperature instability, or low albumin. Family history and Asian heritage support G6PD screening. Intensive multiple phototherapy with adequate hydration should start once the threshold is crossed, with reassessment at 4-6 hours. Continued breastfeeding is supported alongside phototherapy.
key_points: Use age-in-hours charts; do not rely on absolute number alone
Risk factors shift threshold down: G6PD, sepsis, prematurity, DAT+
Intensive phototherapy: multiple banks, maximise skin exposure
Continue breastfeeding; supplement only if weight loss >10 percent
explanation.pearls: G6PD deficiency is X-linked and affects up to 10-15 percent of males in Mediterranean, Southeast Asian, and African populations; oxidative haemolysis can occur without an obvious trigger in neonates because of transient enzyme deficiency in RBC precursors.

options.rationale: At 62 hours and 310 micromol/L with a G6PD deficiency risk factor (Asian ethnicity, family history of exchange), the threshold shifts down and intensive phototherapy is warranted rather than single-bank conventional. (Source: RCH Melbourne Neonatal Jaundice Guideline)

Bilirubin 310 micromol/L at 62 hours with the family history and Asian heritage places this baby above the phototherapy threshold using the RCH lowered risk-factor line; intensive phototherapy with hydration and urgent G6PD assay is indicated. (Source: RCH Melbourne Neonatal Jaundice Guideline)

Exchange thresholds at 62 hours are well above 310 micromol/L on RCH charts even with risk factors; intensive phototherapy is first-line and typically averts exchange when started promptly. (Source: RCH Melbourne Neonatal Jaundice Guideline)

Breast milk jaundice presents later (day 7 onward) and interrupting breastfeeding is not first-line; the current picture is early with a risk factor requiring phototherapy while supporting continued breastfeeding. (Source: RCH Melbourne Neonatal Jaundice Guideline)

The absolute value with risk factors already exceeds the intervention threshold; deferring 12 hours risks bilirubin rising into exchange range and preventable neurotoxicity. (Source: RCH Melbourne Neonatal Jaundice Guideline)

explanation.summary: Intussusception in a child 3 months to 3 years old classically presents with intermittent colicky pain (legs drawn up), quiet interictal periods, vomiting and later red material stools. Ultrasound sensitivity approaches 98 percent in expert hands but a technically limited scan does not exclude the diagnosis. Rising lactate, tachycardia, and drowsiness suggest bowel compromise. Confirm with repeat expert ultrasound and manage with fluid resuscitation, NG decompression, and air enema reduction; laparotomy is reserved for perforation, peritonism, or failed reduction.
key_points: Classic triad: colic, red material stool, sausage-shaped mass
Ultrasound is first-line; a limited scan is not exclusion
Air enema reduction after resuscitation is definitive when no peritonism
Laparotomy for peritonism, perforation, or failed radiological reduction
explanation.pearls: Enema reduction has 85-90 percent success in typical ileocolic intussusception under 48 hours; recurrence rate is around 10 percent, higher after operative reduction than after air enema.

options.rationale: An inconclusive ultrasound (technically limited view) does not exclude intussusception; classic triad plus rising lactate and worsening drowsiness demands repeat imaging or definitive management, not discharge. (Source: RCH Melbourne Intussusception Guideline)

Repeat ultrasound is reasonable but skipping to immediate operative intervention before confirming a diagnosis or attempting radiological reduction is not the standard pathway when the child has no peritonism. (Source: RCH Melbourne Intussusception Guideline)

Plain films have low sensitivity for intussusception and are used to look for perforation, not to make the diagnosis; ultrasound by an experienced operator is the modality of choice. (Source: RCH Melbourne Intussusception Guideline)

Sepsis alone does not fit the intermittent colic with drawing up of legs pattern; treating for sepsis without repeating imaging risks a missed surgical diagnosis and infarcted bowel. (Source: RCH Melbourne Intussusception Guideline)

Classic triad, worsening drowsiness, elevated lactate, and inconclusive first scan warrant repeat imaging with an experienced operator; if intussusception confirmed and no peritonism or perforation, air enema reduction after IV fluids and NG decompression is first-line. (Source: RCH Melbourne Intussusception Guideline)

explanation.summary: Turner syndrome (45,X and mosaic variants) commonly presents with short stature, delayed puberty, and characteristic dysmorphology. A radiofemoral BP gradient and upper limb hypertension flag coarctation of the aorta, present in around 10 percent, alongside bicuspid aortic valve in around 30 percent. Cardiac MRI complements echocardiography to define aortic arch anatomy and dilation risk. Karyotype confirms the diagnosis but should not delay urgent cardiovascular characterisation. Growth hormone, oestrogen induction, and multisystem screening follow.
key_points: Coarctation, bicuspid AV, aortic dilation drive early cardiac priority
TTE plus cardiac MRI (or CT if MRI contraindicated)
Karyotype confirms diagnosis; do not delay imaging
Multisystem screen: renal ultrasound, hearing, thyroid, glucose
explanation.pearls: Aortic dissection lifetime risk in Turner syndrome is around 1 to 2 percent, disproportionately in those with hypertension, bicuspid valve, or coarctation; annual cardiac imaging surveillance is recommended from diagnosis.

options.rationale: Karyotype is essential and should be sent, but the clinical picture is already highly suggestive and immediate priority is characterising the cardiovascular lesion causing radiofemoral BP delay before initiating any therapy. (Source: Turner Syndrome Clinical Practice Guidelines 2017)

Bone age informs growth hormone timing but is not the most urgent step; missing a coarctation risks aortic dissection, and cardiac assessment must precede endocrine therapy planning. (Source: Turner Syndrome Clinical Practice Guidelines 2017)

Pelvic ultrasound informs later fertility counselling and oestrogen induction planning but is not the most urgent investigation given the radiofemoral BP gradient requiring immediate cardiovascular workup. (Source: Turner Syndrome Clinical Practice Guidelines 2017)

Radiofemoral gradient with upper limb hypertension in a phenotypic Turner girl strongly suggests coarctation, present in around 10 percent; bicuspid aortic valve in around 30 percent; TTE plus cardiac MRI is priority to guide urgent intervention and pre-empt aortic dissection risk. (Source: Turner Syndrome Clinical Practice Guidelines 2017)

Renal ultrasound is part of the Turner screening panel (30 to 40 percent have anomalies) but is not more urgent than characterising a suspected coarctation causing measurable BP gradient. (Source: Turner Syndrome Clinical Practice Guidelines 2017)

explanation.summary: Shunt malfunction in a chronic shunt patient must be diagnosed clinically, not by imaging alone. Slit-ventricle physiology and partial obstruction can produce raised ICP with unchanged CT ventricular size. Morning headache, vomiting, papilloedema, sixth nerve palsy, ataxia, and parental pattern-recognition are the syndrome. MRI (with or without shunt-flow sequences) and neurosurgical shunt tap measure function directly. Lumbar puncture is contraindicated because tonsillar herniation risk is high with outflow obstruction.
key_points: Diagnose shunt malfunction clinically, not by CT alone
Slit-ventricle syndrome has minimal ventricular change
Neurosurgical shunt tap and MRI are diagnostic
Avoid LP in obstructive shunt failure
explanation.pearls: Around 40 percent of paediatric shunts fail within 2 years and 50 percent within 5 years; median shunt survival is 6 years, with obstruction the commonest cause followed by infection and disconnection.

options.rationale: Papilloedema, morning vomiting, ataxia and diplopia with the mother's previous shunt-failure pattern are classic raised ICP even with unchanged imaging; discharge risks decompensation and death. (Source: RCH Melbourne VP Shunt Guideline)

Imaging can appear unchanged in slit-ventricle physiology or partial obstruction; the syndrome (papilloedema, ataxia, diplopia, mother's pattern recognition) mandates neurosurgical shunt tap for ICP measurement and MRI to reassess, not repeat plain imaging alone. (Source: RCH Melbourne VP Shunt Guideline)

Lumbar puncture in suspected obstructive shunt malfunction risks tonsillar herniation because CSF flow around the outflow obstruction may be compromised; it is contraindicated as a first step. (Source: RCH Melbourne VP Shunt Guideline)

Mannitol without a plan for definitive shunt evaluation delays diagnosis; the priority is neurosurgical assessment with shunt tap and MRI, and empirical osmotic therapy is reserved for herniation signs. (Source: RCH Melbourne VP Shunt Guideline)

Repeating CT without neurosurgical shunt evaluation misses functional obstruction with minimal ventricular change (slit-ventricle syndrome); MRI plus shunt tap by neurosurgery is required. (Source: RCH Melbourne VP Shunt Guideline)

explanation.summary: Salt-losing congenital adrenal hyperplasia (usually 21-hydroxylase deficiency) classically presents around 1-3 weeks of life with vomiting, poor feeding, dehydration, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, and hypoglycaemia. Virilised external genitalia in a 46,XX infant may be missed or attributed to birth trauma. Newborn screening detects most but results are not always available at presentation. Immediate treatment is 0.9 percent saline for volume, IV dextrose for hypoglycaemia, and stress-dose IV hydrocortisone (25 mg in infants; 50 mg in children; 100 mg in adolescents) before biochemistry confirmation. Take pre-treatment blood for 17-OHP, cortisol, ACTH, renin, and electrolytes.
key_points: Salt-losing crisis: hypoNa, hyperK, hypoglycaemia, acidosis
Fluid: 0.9 percent saline bolus with dextrose; avoid hypotonic
Hydrocortisone 25 mg IV in infants stat (do not wait)
Draw pre-treatment 17-OHP, cortisol, ACTH, renin
explanation.pearls: Hydrocortisone at high dose has intrinsic mineralocorticoid activity through renal glucocorticoid receptor spillover; fludrocortisone is added enterally for maintenance once absorption is reliable, not during crisis.

sources.label: Endocrine Society CAH Clinical Practice Guideline 2018

options.rationale: Salt-losing CAH crisis needs volume with 0.9 percent saline (avoid hypotonic), IV glucose for hypoglycaemia, and IV hydrocortisone 25 mg stat for the infant regardless of exact dose calculation while endocrine advice is sought; this is the RCH salt-losing crisis pathway. (Source: RCH Melbourne CAH Guideline)

Hypotonic fluid worsens the hyponatraemia; oral fludrocortisone is too slow and unreliable in a vomiting infant; IV hydrocortisone provides the acute glucocorticoid plus mineralocorticoid activity needed at stress dose. (Source: RCH Melbourne CAH Guideline)

Hypertonic saline is reserved for seizures or severe symptomatic hyponatraemia; in salt-losing crisis, volume replacement with 0.9 percent saline plus hydrocortisone corrects sodium physiologically without rapid rise and osmotic demyelination risk. (Source: RCH Melbourne CAH Guideline)

Insulin-dextrose shift risks worsening the already-low glucose; hyperkalaemia in salt-losing CAH corrects with volume replacement plus hydrocortisone acting on the aldosterone-deficient state; insulin shift is a distraction and dangerous here. (Source: RCH Melbourne CAH Guideline)

Waiting for 17-OHP results before treating a shocked hypoglycaemic infant with virilisation and salt-wasting picture would risk arrest; treat empirically and confirm biochemistry after resuscitation samples are drawn. (Source: RCH Melbourne CAH Guideline)

explanation.summary: Bacterial epiglottitis is rare since Hib vaccination but resurgent in unvaccinated children. The classic triad is drooling, muffled voice and dysphagia with a rapid febrile onset and no cough. Management priority is airway preservation - minimise handling, no cannulation attempts, no examination of the throat, transfer with the parent to theatre for gaseous induction by an experienced paediatric anaesthetist with ENT stand-by for surgical airway. IV ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg follows definitive airway control. Household contacts require rifampicin prophylaxis if any contact is under four and unimmunised.
key_points: Drooling, muffled voice, no cough and toxic look = epiglottitis until proven otherwise
Minimal handling; do not lie flat; do not cannulate before theatre
Anaesthetics + ENT in theatre with surgical airway back-up
Ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg IV after airway secure
Rifampicin prophylaxis for unimmunised household contacts under four
explanation.pearls: Consider parainfluenza-mediated bacterial tracheitis in a similar-looking child with cough and thick pus at the trachea on laryngoscopy - IV flucloxacillin plus ceftriaxone is the AU empirical cover.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Acute upper airway obstruction

options.rationale: This is the RCH management pathway for severe croup, which presents with barking cough and coryzal prodrome. Rapid onset with drooling, muffled voice and toxicity without cough points to epiglottitis, where instrumentation risks complete obstruction and paediatric anaesthetic-led intubation in theatre is the safe approach. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute upper airway obstruction)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Acute upper airway obstruction

options.rationale: Lateral neck imaging is unnecessary and dangerous - the child must lie back for the film and the film is not diagnostic in a proportion of cases. Bedside clinical assessment plus theatre laryngoscopy is the standard, and imaging causes delay. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute upper airway obstruction)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Acute upper airway obstruction

options.rationale: Antibiotic cover with ceftriaxone is appropriate once the airway is definitively secured, but cannulation prior to airway control commonly precipitates crying, complete obstruction and cardiac arrest in suspected epiglottitis. Antibiotics follow the airway, not the other way round. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute upper airway obstruction)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Acute upper airway obstruction

options.rationale: Toxic child, drooling, muffled voice, absent cough and unvaccinated for Hib fit epiglottitis. Any distress can precipitate complete obstruction, so the safe plan is minimal handling, no throat inspection, keep upright with the parent, and rapid escalation to a senior team who can secure the airway in theatre with a surgical airway back-up. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute upper airway obstruction)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Acute upper airway obstruction

options.rationale: High flow nasal cannula does not treat mechanical supraglottic obstruction and delays theatre transfer. In epiglottitis, oxygen without airway control does not prevent obstruction. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute upper airway obstruction)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Acute upper airway obstruction

explanation.summary: Prolonged jaundice beyond 14 days in a term infant (21 days if preterm) mandates a split bilirubin. A conjugated fraction above 25 micromol/L or above 20 percent of total defines cholestasis and demands same-day tertiary transfer to exclude biliary atresia. Acholic stools and dark urine are hallmark features. Kasai hepatoportoenterostomy performed before day 45 to 60 of life gives the best chance of a native liver, so time to diagnosis directly determines outcome. Never delay imaging or refer for outpatient follow-up when the split bilirubin is abnormal.
key_points: Conjugated bilirubin >25 micromol/L or >20 percent of total = cholestasis
Pale acholic stools + cholestasis = biliary atresia until proven otherwise
Kasai portoenterostomy outcomes decline sharply after day 60
Same-day tertiary hepatology transfer, not clinic review
Phototherapy has no role in conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia
explanation.pearls: Give IM vitamin K 1 mg on transfer to any infant with cholestasis regardless of prior IM dose, because bile-dependent vitamin K absorption is impaired and intracranial haemorrhage risk is real.

options.rationale: Breast milk jaundice is entirely unconjugated. A conjugated bilirubin above 25 micromol/L or above 20 percent of total demands urgent workup regardless of how well the infant appears - pale stools plus a raised conjugated fraction is biliary atresia until proven otherwise. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

Empirical UDCA in an undifferentiated cholestatic neonate delays diagnosis and does not treat biliary atresia. Symptomatic pharmacotherapy is only appropriate once biliary atresia is excluded and a specific diagnosis (e.g. Alagille syndrome, PFIC) is made. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

Conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia (42 micromol/L is above the 25 micromol/L threshold) with acholic stools in a 22-day-old is a paediatric emergency. Kasai portoenterostomy outcomes are best when performed before day 45 to 60 of life, so any hint of biliary atresia mandates same-day transfer for HIDA scan, targeted ultrasound and liver biopsy under a paediatric hepatology team. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

Phototherapy addresses unconjugated bilirubin only and does not treat conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia. Using phototherapy here is inappropriate and dangerously delays biliary atresia workup. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

TORCH and TSH form part of the cholestatic workup but they are done in parallel with tertiary transfer, not instead of it. Waiting five days for outpatient results erodes the window for a successful Kasai procedure. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

explanation.summary: A simple febrile convulsion is generalised, lasts under 15 minutes, occurs once in 24 hours, and happens in a child aged 6 months to 5 years with fever and no CNS infection or metabolic disturbance. Recovery to baseline is expected within an hour. Investigation is by clinical judgement for the source of fever, not for the seizure. Discharge home is appropriate if baseline is regained, there is a clear infective source and no red flags. Parental education and a written action plan reduce anxiety and prompt appropriate re-presentation for prolonged recurrence.
key_points: Simple: generalised, <15 min, one in 24 hours, age 6 months to 5 years
No EEG, no MRI, no anticonvulsants for simple seizures
LP only for <12 months, atypical features, meningism or prior antibiotics
Antipyretics do not prevent recurrence but treat discomfort
Recurrence risk ~30 percent overall; higher if first seizure under 18 months
explanation.pearls: Buccal midazolam 0.3 mg/kg (max 10 mg) is the AU home-treatment agent for a subsequent seizure lasting over 5 minutes; it replaces rectal diazepam in most Australian paediatric services.

options.rationale: Simple febrile seizures do not need EEG or MRI. Routine admission is not required if the child has returned to baseline, has a clear infective source and there are no atypical features. Investigations are reserved for complex, prolonged or focal seizures. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile convulsion)

A simple febrile convulsion (generalised, under 15 min, one in 24 hours) in a child aged 6 months to 5 years who has returned to baseline can be discharged home with parental education, safety-netting for recurrence, and a plain-language written action plan. Antipyretics do not prevent recurrence but treat discomfort. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile convulsion)

Lumbar puncture is reserved for infants under twelve months, any child with meningism, atypical features, or those on prior antibiotics that could mask meningitis. An 18-month-old with normal neurology and clear alternative source does not need LP. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile convulsion)

Prophylactic anticonvulsants are not indicated for simple febrile convulsions. Recurrence risk is around 30 percent but the majority are benign and self-limited. Valproate carries significant hepatotoxicity and teratogenicity risks not justified here. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile convulsion)

Prophylactic benzodiazepines with fever are not standard AU practice. Buccal midazolam is supplied only for children with recurrent prolonged seizures over 5 minutes as part of an individualised seizure action plan, not first presentation. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile convulsion)

explanation.summary: TEN-4-FACESp is the AU-endorsed screening rule for suspicious bruising in children under four - bruises to the Torso, Ears, Neck, Frenulum, Angle of the jaw, Cheeks, Eyes and Sclera, and any bruise in a child under 4 months, warrant safeguarding referral. Faltering growth and inconsistent history add weight. Mandatory reporting is a legal obligation across all Australian jurisdictions and does not require certainty of abuse - a reasonable suspicion suffices. Admission ensures safety, formal photographs, skeletal survey (age under 2), coagulation screen, and multidisciplinary child protection review. Discussion with the alleged perpetrator is contraindicated.
key_points: TEN-4-FACESp bruising rule triggers safeguarding referral
Mandatory reporting is a legal duty across all AU states and territories
Admit for skeletal survey, coagulation screen, and MDT review
Never discuss suspicion with the possible perpetrator
Faltering growth adds weight to the safeguarding concern
explanation.pearls: In any child under 2 with unexplained bruising or suspected inflicted injury, arrange a formal skeletal survey with follow-up survey at 10 to 14 days to detect healing rib and metaphyseal fractures invisible on the first film.

options.rationale: Clinical photographs must be taken on hospital-approved medical photography systems and are part of the medical record, not the family's. This option also fails the mandatory reporting duty. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)

This misses mandatory reporting and safeguarding obligations. Bruises in the ears, cheeks and buttocks in a young child are not typical of accidental household injury and cannot be discharged without formal safeguarding assessment. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)

Excluding a bleeding disorder is part of the workup but not a substitute for safeguarding. Discharge home while suspicion is unresolved returns the child to potential harm; mandatory reporting is a legal obligation and does not depend on excluding all medical mimics first. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)

Interrogating or informing a suspected perpetrator can jeopardise the investigation and the child's safety. Concerns are shared with the mandated statutory service, not with adults in the household about whom concerns exist. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)

Bruising in a non-mobile or barely-mobile infant in high-risk sites (cheeks, pinnae, patterned marks) with faltering growth and inconsistent history meets mandatory reporting criteria. Admission enables safety, investigation (skeletal survey, coagulation, head imaging as clinically indicated) and multidisciplinary assessment. Australian state law makes registered medical practitioners mandatory reporters of suspected significant harm. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)

explanation.summary: Classic Kawasaki disease requires fever for at least 4 days plus 4 of 5 principal features (bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis, oral mucosal changes, polymorphous rash, extremity changes, cervical lymphadenopathy). Incomplete Kawasaki disease is diagnosed when fever plus 2-3 principal features are present alongside supportive laboratory findings (CRP >30 mg/L, ESR >40 mm/hr, platelets >450 x10^9/L, WBC >15 x10^9/L, ALT elevated, sterile pyuria, hypoalbuminaemia, anaemia). Any infant under 6 months with fever over 7 days and no cause found should be assessed for incomplete Kawasaki disease. IVIG 2 g/kg plus aspirin within 10 days of fever onset reduces coronary artery aneurysm risk from around 25 percent to 5 percent.
key_points: Fever ≥4 days plus 4/5 principal features = classic Kawasaki disease
Fever + 2-3 features + supportive labs = incomplete Kawasaki disease
IVIG 2 g/kg + aspirin within 10 days of fever onset
Echocardiography before, then 2 and 6 weeks post-treatment
Steroids are adjunctive in high-risk or IVIG-refractory patients
explanation.pearls: Kobayashi score >4 identifies IVIG-resistant patients at Australian centres; primary IVIG plus prednisolone (RAISE trial) reduces coronary complications versus IVIG alone in this high-risk subgroup.

options.rationale: Fever is already at day seven, satisfying the temporal criterion for classic and incomplete Kawasaki disease.
