Continued observation risks coronary artery aneurysm formation - the therapeutic window for IVIG to reduce aneurysm risk is within the first 10 days of illness. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

Corticosteroid monotherapy is not the first-line Kawasaki treatment. Steroids are used in addition to IVIG in high-risk patients or as adjunctive therapy for IVIG-resistant disease (Kobayashi risk score), never as sole first-line therapy. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

Refusal to weight-bear could suggest septic arthritis but the constellation of persistent fever, mucocutaneous features, marked thrombocytosis and sterile pyuria points to Kawasaki disease. Empirical antibiotics with no source and specific Kawasaki features delays IVIG. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

This child has incomplete Kawasaki disease - prolonged fever with only two of five classic mucocutaneous features (rash, cracked lip) plus supportive laboratory criteria (raised CRP over 30 mg/L, ESR over 40 mm/hr, thrombocytosis over 450, albumin under 30, ALT elevated, sterile pyuria, anaemia). AHA criteria for infants under 6 months with unexplained fever over 7 days also include this presentation. Treat with IVIG plus high-dose aspirin without waiting for classic features. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

High-dose aspirin (30-50 mg/kg/day in divided doses is the AHA range) is co-administered with IVIG for its anti-inflammatory effect until afebrile 48 hours, then reduced to antiplatelet dose. Reye syndrome risk relates to viral illness co-administration; benefits of aspirin in Kawasaki disease outweigh this and treatment is not withheld. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

explanation.summary: Classic salt-wasting CAH (21-hydroxylase deficiency, 75 percent of CAH cases) presents in the second to third week of life with vomiting, poor feeding, weight loss, shock, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and hypoglycaemia. 46,XX infants may have ambiguous genitalia noted at birth; 46,XY infants appear phenotypically normal and are more likely to present in crisis before diagnosis. Australian NBS now includes 17-OHP but results may not return before crisis onset. Immediate management is 20 mL/kg 0.9 percent saline bolus, IV hydrocortisone at stress dose (25 mg for neonate, 50 mg for infant/toddler, 100 mg for older child), correction of hypoglycaemia, and paediatric endocrinology involvement.
key_points: Week 2-3 vomiting, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia = salt-wasting CAH
20 mL/kg saline bolus + IV hydrocortisone (25/50/100 mg by age)
Draw 17-OHP, cortisol, ACTH, aldosterone, renin BEFORE first hydrocortisone dose
Fludrocortisone (oral only) starts once oral tolerance returns
Family require genetic counselling; sibling screening
explanation.pearls: In male 46,XY infants with no genital ambiguity, unexplained neonatal shock with hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia should always trigger consideration of CAH before attributing collapse to sepsis alone.

sources.label: Australasian Paediatric Endocrine Group CAH guidance

options.rationale: Insulin-dextrose treats life-threatening hyperkalaemia (with ECG changes) but the primary derangement here is aldosterone deficiency causing hyponatraemic dehydration and hyperkalaemia. Volume resuscitation with saline and hydrocortisone corrects both derangements causally. (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia)

Salt-wasting congenital adrenal hyperplasia crisis in a 46,XX neonate with virilisation presents in week 2 to 3 with vomiting, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia and shock. Immediate resuscitation is 20 mL/kg 0.9 percent saline bolus, stress-dose hydrocortisone (25 mg for a neonate; 50 mg for an infant/toddler; 100 mg for older children), and glucose correction. Fludrocortisone can wait until oral tolerance is regained. (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia)

Rapid correction of chronic hyponatraemia risks osmotic demyelination. The hyponatraemia of salt-wasting CAH corrects with 0.9 percent saline plus mineralocorticoid activity restored by hydrocortisone; hypertonic saline is reserved for symptomatic seizures or coma from acute hyponatraemia. (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia)

Empirical hydrocortisone is life-saving and does not compromise diagnostic testing if 17-OHP and other adrenal steroids are drawn before the first dose. Waiting for results in a shocked neonate is unacceptable. (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia)

Fludrocortisone has no parenteral form and takes days to act. Acute salt-wasting crisis needs IV volume resuscitation and IV hydrocortisone, which has intrinsic mineralocorticoid activity at stress doses. (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia)

explanation.summary: The Australian paediatric sepsis pathway (RCH-adapted from ANZICS and SCCM) is: recognise sepsis, IV/IO access within 5 minutes, blood cultures, IV antibiotic within 60 minutes, 20 mL/kg 0.9 percent saline bolus repeated to a 40-60 mL/kg ceiling. If shock persists after 40 mL/kg, start peripheral or IO adrenaline infusion at 0.05 micrograms/kg/min and titrate. Central access and intubation follow. Dopamine is no longer first-line. Continued unmonitored fluid pushes past 60 mL/kg increases mortality via cerebral oedema and pulmonary compromise. Bedside echocardiography and inferior vena cava assessment help guide further fluid needs.
key_points: 40-60 mL/kg is the initial fluid ceiling; start adrenaline early after
Adrenaline preferred over dopamine as first-line vasoactive
Peripheral/IO vasoactive is safe while awaiting central access
Ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg IV within 60 minutes for meningococcal sepsis
Intubation anticipated for fluid-refractory shock
explanation.pearls: Purpura fulminans mandates urgent haematology involvement and consideration of activated protein C or protein C concentrate replacement in severe meningococcal septicaemia; skin necrosis extension can amputate limbs.

options.rationale: After one bolus with only partial response, the second bolus is given while starting peripheral adrenaline infusion (0.05-0.3 microgram/kg/min) rather than waiting for the 60 mL/kg ceiling. Fluid-refractory shock is defined as persistent hypoperfusion after 40 mL/kg, and vasoactives should be started early via peripheral IV or IO whilst central access is being obtained. Intubation and central line are anticipated. (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis)

Australian and international paediatric sepsis guidance limits initial crystalloid resuscitation to 40-60 mL/kg total, and mandates early adrenaline for fluid-refractory shock at that ceiling. Continued boluses beyond 40 mL/kg without vasoactive support increases mortality from pulmonary oedema and worsens outcome. (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis)

The 2020 Surviving Sepsis paediatric update and Australian centres now prefer adrenaline over dopamine as first-line vasoactive in septic shock; dopamine is associated with worse outcomes. Both agents can be run peripherally short-term while central access is obtained. (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis)

Stress-dose hydrocortisone is considered in fluid- and catecholamine-resistant shock or where adrenal insufficiency is suspected; it does not precede fluid and vasoactive resuscitation. Empirical Waterhouse-Friderichsen prophylaxis is not standard practice ahead of stabilisation. (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis)

Blood transfusion in septic shock is guided by haemoglobin and haemorrhagic loss, not initial resuscitation. Sepsis-3 guidance targets Hb >70 g/L in stable septic patients. Empirical blood without indication delays evidence-based care. (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis)

explanation.summary: Intussusception peaks between 3 months and 3 years and typically presents with intermittent colicky pain, drawing up of legs, vomiting (later becoming bilious), and passage of red-currant stool (a late sign). Pneumatic (air) enema reduction under fluoroscopy achieves 80-90 percent success in uncomplicated cases and is first-line if the child is stable, well perfused, no peritonism, symptoms less than 24 hours and no radiological signs of ischaemia. Peritonism, shock, bilious vomiting, prolonged history, and ultrasound signs of ischaemia mandate resuscitation, broad-spectrum antibiotics, and surgical reduction (often requiring resection). Recurrence after enema is 10 percent.
key_points: Air enema first-line if stable and no peritonism/ischaemia
Peritonism, shock, bilious vomiting = surgery, not enema
Fluid resuscitation + antibiotics + NG tube + surgical referral
Pathological lead points (Meckel's, polyp) more likely in age >3 years
Recurrence after enema ~10 percent, warn parents
explanation.pearls: In a child over 3 years or with recurrent intussusception, look actively for a pathological lead point (Meckel's diverticulum, lymphoma, polyp) - the routine idiopathic intussusception explanation does not apply.

options.rationale: Peritonism, shock, ischaemic ultrasound findings and bilious vomiting are absolute contraindications to pneumatic reduction because perforation risk is prohibitive. Air enema requires a stable child with a viable intussusceptum and no peritonism. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

Barium reduction carries greater peritoneal contamination risk than air if perforation occurs and is not preferred in the AU practice. Both are absolutely contraindicated in the presence of peritonism regardless of contrast type. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

This child has complicated intussusception with peritonism, shock, and lactic acidosis - all contraindications to non-operative reduction. Management is aggressive volume resuscitation, broad-spectrum antibiotics covering enteric organisms, gastric decompression via NG tube, and immediate paediatric surgical referral for laparotomy with manual reduction or resection. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

Observation of a shocked child with peritonism and ischaemic ultrasound findings is negligent. Spontaneous reduction may occur in mild uncomplicated cases but is never watched-for in a patient with any surgical acute abdomen findings. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

The first step is resuscitation with fluids and antibiotics with gastric decompression - definitive operative approach (open versus laparoscopic) is a surgical decision after stabilisation. Jumping directly to a specific operative approach bypasses resuscitation priorities. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)
